meta.note: Test fixture: a large synthetic climbing-and-triathlon programme (31 session cards, 6 tests, 11 quota categories) that the test suites render and check against. Not loaded by the app; examples/plan.json and content/starter.json are generated from it by app/starter.build.mjs.

testingNotes.title: Two instruments, two jobs — do not mix their numbers
testingNotes.body: The Port-A-Board on the load cell and a bodyweight hang measure related but NON-interchangeable things, and no published equation converts between them. So each gets one job. The BLOCK + TINDEQ is your measuring instrument: peak force, tested every 3 weeks, because peak force has a CV of about 5.6% and is the most precise number you will own. The HANGBOARD with counterweight is your training tool, because every protocol in this plan was validated on hangs, not block pulls. Set training loads from your hang max; track progress on the block. Two separate series in the log. Never compare one to the other, and never switch a series mid-block.

testingNotes.title: Read this before you test anything
testingNotes.body: Two numbers matter and one is a trap. Peak force on a max hang has a coefficient of variation around 5.6% — it is the most trackable thing you own. Critical Force has a CV of 21% with 95% limits of agreement from −62.6% to +58.1% (McClean 2023), which means a single retest showing +20% is statistically indistinguishable from no change. Track peak force. Treat any endurance change under roughly 15% as noise, not progress.

testingNotes.title: Fix the configuration and never touch it
testingNotes.body: Four published CF protocols use four different setups — one arm vs two, 20mm vs 23mm, shaking allowed vs forbidden, mean-of-last-three vs minimum-of-last-three. Cross-setup comparison is meaningless. Only self-versus-self on a fixed configuration tells you anything. Pick your edge, grip, duration and rest now, write them down, and keep them identical for eleven weeks.

testingNotes.title: Your baseline already says something important
testingNotes.body: A max hang near the population median for your bouldering grade is common. Within your own ability band, max hang explains under 10% of grade variance anyway.

tests.name: MVC-7 — max hang anchor
tests.why: The one number precise enough to track month to month (CV ≈ 5.6%). It anchors every intensity in the program: your repeater loads are percentages of this. Retest it and the whole plan re-scales.
tests.equipment: 20mm rung, harness, pulley or weight belt, plates. Load cell optional — if you use one, use it every time, never mix methods.
procedure: Warm up properly: 10 min easy movement, then 3–4 progressively heavier hangs (bodyweight, then ~50%, ~70%, ~85% of your expected max) with 2 min rest between.
Rest 5 minutes.
Attempt 1: load to roughly your last known max. Hang 7 seconds, two arms, half crimp, arms slightly bent, shoulders engaged.
Rest 3–5 minutes between every attempt. This is a strength test — under-resting makes it an endurance test.
Add 5–10 lb and repeat until you cannot hold a clean 7 seconds. Maximum 5 attempts total.
Record the heaviest load you held for a full clean 7 seconds. Stop there — do not chase a number on a sixth attempt.
cautions: Do not test on a fresh-skin day and compare it to a shredded-skin day. Note skin condition.
Do not change edge, grip position, or hang duration between tests.
Do not test more often than every 4–5 weeks. Weekly testing produces noise you will then react to.
tests.interpretation: Because 7s is an easier test than 10s, your MVC-7 number will read higher — do not compare the two. A change smaller than about 6%  is inside the noise band. Maintenance is a win during this block; you are not trying to add strength here.

tests.name: Peak force — Tindeq + Port-A-Board
tests.why: The most precise number you own (CV ≈ 5.6%, versus 21% for critical force). This is the one that tells you whether the block is working. Available from Mon 10 Aug once you have familiarised.
tests.equipment: Tindeq Progressor 200, Frictitious Port-A-Board on its rated cord, a sling or foot loop to anchor to the floor, a carabiner.
procedure: Anchor the gauge to the floor with a sling under your foot. Block clipped to the other end.
Stand tall, arm at your side, elbow slightly bent. Same body position EVERY time — write down where your feet are.
Warm up: 3 progressively harder pulls (~50%, 70%, 85%) with 1 min between.
Rest 3 minutes.
20mm edge, half crimp, ONE hand at a time. Pull to max over about 2 seconds and hold for 5.
3 attempts per hand, 3 minutes rest between every attempt.
Record the best of 3 for each hand, and the average of left and right.
cautions: Same body position, same edge, same grip, same time of day. Any change makes the series worthless.
This counts as one of your hard finger exposures that week — at most three, never two days running.
Do not test more often than every 3 weeks.
Never compare this number to your hang numbers. Different instruments, no conversion exists.
tests.interpretation: Track the average. A change under about 6% is inside the noise band. Left/right asymmetry over about 10% is worth noting but not worth panicking over. Maintenance across this block is a win; you are not trying to add strength here.

tests.name: Critical force — 4-min all-out
tests.why: Max hangs measure the engine you already have; critical force measures the boundary between an intensity you can hold indefinitely and one that is quietly draining you — which is the thing that decides whether you arrive at the rest on a 5.12a with anything left. It is also the number every sub-threshold session in this plan is dosed against, so without it those sessions are a guess at a percentage rather than a measured boundary.
tests.equipment: Tindeq Progressor 200 + Frictitious Port-A-Board on the 20 mm edge, rigged exactly as on the calibration day — webbing loop under both feet or the floor eye bolt, standing tall, working arm straight down at your side, wrist neutral, four fingers half crimp, thumb off. The Progressor app has this test built in; use its Critical Force mode rather than timing it yourself.
procedure: Do this FRESH. Not within 48 h of hard climbing, and not after the max-pull attempts unless you have rested at least 10 minutes — better still, give it its own day.
Warm up as for the calibration day: general warmth first, then ascending 5-second pulls at roughly 20 / 40 / 60 / 80% with 60 s between, then 2 minutes of full rest.
Same arm every time. The protocol is the dominant arm only; testing the other one later does not give you a comparable series.
Open the app's Critical Force test: 24 repetitions of 7 seconds maximal pull / 3 seconds rest, 4 minutes continuous.

Pull as hard as you can on EVERY rep, including the first. Do not pace yourself — pacing invalidates the test. The force is supposed to fall steeply for the first ~2 minutes and then flatten out, and the flat part is the entire point.
Between reps let go completely and shake the hand out at your side. Leaving the hand resting on the edge changes the measurement.
Read off: CF (mean end-test force, what the app reports), CFmin (the lowest single contraction of the final three), and the impulse above end-test force (the app labels this W').
Record the same-day max for the arm you tested, so CF can be read as a percentage of it. That ratio is more informative than the raw kilograms.
Do not repeat more often than every 4–6 weeks. See the caution about noise below — retesting more often mostly measures the test.
cautions: Any sharp finger pain, a pop, a click, or pain at the finger joint creases — stop immediately and do not finish the test.
Numbness or tingling in the fingers.
Medial or lateral elbow pain that builds across the four minutes.
Do not run this pre-fatigued. It is worthless within 48 h of hard climbing, and it is a genuinely hard finger exposure in its own right — budget it as one.
Do not change the rig between tests. Arm position materially changes measured finger force, so a new setup starts a new series.

metrics.label: CFmin — lowest of the final three contractions
Impulse above end-test force (the app calls this W')
Same-day max on the arm you tested

tests.interpretation:
Three readings, in order of how much you should trust them.

CF AS A FRACTION OF YOUR MAX is the one that matters for this block. Fryer et al. 2019 put critical force at 41.0 ± 6.2% of MVC in climbers. Below that band means your ceiling is limited by endurance rather than by strength — which is exactly the deficit this block exists to fix, and exactly what you should expect to see move. The signature of the plan working is CF and CF-as-%-of-max rising while max stays flat. Max rising and CF flat means you have accidentally turned the sub-threshold work into strength work.

YOUR TRAINING CEILING comes out of this test and nothing else. Baláš et al. 2024 (n=12) showed the reported CF overestimates what is actually sustainable: at calculated CF only one of twelve climbers lasted the full 12-minute trial, and completion rose to 38% at CF−2 kg, 69% at CF−4 kg and 92% at CF−6 kg. So the working ceiling is CFmin, or CF−6 kg, whichever is LOWER, and every sub-threshold session is prescribed against that in absolute kilograms.

THE ABSOLUTE NUMBER IS NOISY, and you should hold it loosely. McClean et al. 2023 (n=13) measured test-retest of this exact 4-minute protocol at ICC 0.848 but a coefficient of variation of 21.0% for end-test force — so a swing of a fifth of the number is within the noise of the test, not a training response. The impulse figure is a little tighter at 13.2% but still not a number to plan around. Retest every 4–6 weeks, read the trend across three tests rather than the gap between two, and never rebuild the block on a single result.

Why bother with a metric this noisy: CF/body mass and W'/body mass together explained 66% of sport-climbing performance in Giles et al. 2021 (n=129), against 44% for bouldering. It is cross-sectional — an association, not proof that raising CF raises your grade — but no other number available to you at home tracks the thing this block is trying to change.

tests.name: 7:3 repeaters to failure at 60% MVC-7
tests.why: The cheap, repeatable finger-endurance number. It is noisy, so it only earns its place if you refuse to over-read it — but it is the closest thing to a direct measure of the deficit you are actually training.
tests.equipment: Same 20mm rung and the same loading method as MVC-7. Counterweight via pulley to hit 60%. A bucket of sand is a perfectly good counterweight.
procedure: Calculate 60% of your MVC-7 total load. Set counterweight so you are hanging exactly that.
Warm up as for a normal session — do not arrive cold, and do not arrive pumped.
Hang 7 seconds, rest 3 seconds, repeat. Chalk between reps is fine.
Do NOT shake your hands or forearms during the 3-second rests. Shaking measurably aids recovery and would make the score depend on how much you shook.
Continue until you cannot complete a full 7-second hang. Stop the clock there.
Record total time under tension in seconds, and the number of completed 7s reps.
cautions: Shaking during rests invalidates the test.
This is genuinely exhausting and skin-limited on wood. Do not run it in the last 10 days before the trip.
Treat anything under a 15% change as noise. Time-to-exhaustion tests carry CVs above 10%, and up to 22.9% on fingerboards.
tests.interpretation: Giles et al. (2019) measured 235 ± 150 s at 60% in elite 7b–8b+ males — note the standard deviation is nearly as large as the mean, which tells you how much individual variation there is. Do not read your number against theirs. Read it against your own, and only believe a change bigger than ~15%.

tests.name: Tension Board repeated-ascent test
tests.why: The single best whole-body climbing test that exists: inter-session reliability around r = .99 and validity around r = .87 with climbing ability. It is also the one test that measures the thing you actually care about — recovering and going again.
tests.equipment: Tension Board at a FIXED angle you will reuse every time. Pick one boulder about two grades below your limit and never change it.
procedure: Set the board to your chosen angle. Write the angle and the exact boulder name down — this is the configuration you are locked into for the block.
Warm up thoroughly, including two easy ascents of the test boulder.
Rest 5 minutes.
Climb the boulder. Start a 2-minute clock the moment you start climbing.
At 2 minutes, climb it again. Repeat on that 2-minute cycle.
Continue until you fail to top it. Record the number of successful ascents.
If you get past 12 ascents, the boulder is too easy — pick a harder one and treat that as a new baseline.
cautions: Never change the board angle or the boulder mid-block. That resets your baseline to zero.
Do not run this on the same day as a hangboard test.
tests.interpretation: There is no published normative table for this — anyone who gives you one is inventing it. Its value is entirely self-referenced, and its reliability is high enough that a change of 2 ascents is real rather than noise.

tests.name: Fixed-time autobelay lap test
tests.why: A fixed-WORK format, which is the point: counting laps in a fixed 12 minutes has a CV under 5%, versus over 10% for climb-until-you-fall. It is the most trustworthy endurance number available to you, and it runs on the vertical autobelay wall you actually have.
tests.equipment: One autobelay route, roughly 5.9–5.10−, that you can reliably climb pumped. 45ft wall. A timer.
procedure: Pick a route and write down the wall, colour and grade. This is fixed for the block.
Warm up, then rest 5 minutes.
Start a 12-minute clock. Climb the route, ride the autobelay down, and immediately start again.
Do not rest on the ground beyond the time it takes to pull the belay down and step back on.
Count completed laps. A partial lap counts as the fraction of the route you reached, to the nearest quarter.
Record laps and your RPE at the end.
cautions: If the gym resets that route, your baseline is gone — pick the closest equivalent and note it as a new baseline rather than pretending it is comparable.
This is a submaximal test. If you are going to failure you picked too hard a route.
tests.interpretation: No normative data exists for this and none is needed. Fixed-work beats time-to-failure precisely because it is repeatable: a one-lap change here means more than a 30-second change on a hang-to-failure test.

dailyMenu.name: Sub-threshold hangs
dailyMenu.dose: 25–30mm rung, load-cell verified at ≤50% of your measured max. 5 × 20–30s, 1 min rest. Should feel easy. If it doesn't, it's too heavy — this day is not supposed to cost you anything.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Pick this on any non-Monday, non-Thursday day. Also the right answer the day after a hard session, or any time your fingers feel even slightly off.

protocol.duration: 8–10 min, no warm-up needed beyond the first set
setup: 25mm or 30mm rung — NOT the 20mm.
Counterweight or feet on the floor.
Load cell on if you have it: this day is defined by staying under a number.
warmup: The first set IS the warm-up. Start easy and stay easy.

blocks.name: Sub-threshold hangs
steps: 5 × 20–30 second hangs on the 25 or 30mm.
1 minute rest between each. There is no rush.
Open hand or half crimp, whichever feels better today. This is not the day to be strict.
You should be able to hold a conversation. If you can't, it's too heavy.

cues: This day is supposed to cost you nothing. If it feels like training, you've loaded it wrong.
The point is blood flow and tissue contact, not stimulus. Under-doing it is the correct error.
stopIf: Anything hurts.
You find yourself gritting your teeth — drop the load 20% and restart.
log: Load used
That's it

outputs.label: Hard finger day?
outputs.hint: This is the answer the budget counts — not what the session was planned as. Two a week, three at a push, never two days running.

how.gist: Easy 25-second hangs on the big rung. Should feel like nothing.
steps: 25 or 30 mm rung — not the 20.
Take weight off: feet on the floor, or counterweight.
Hang 25 seconds. Open hand or half crimp, whichever feels better.
Rest a minute. Five hangs and you are done.
how.watch: If you couldn't hold a conversation through it, it is too heavy.

dailyMenu.name: Grip economy drill
dailyMenu.dose: On the board or a wall: open hand only, no re-gripping, the loosest grip that still holds, silent feet. Full one-hand-off shakeout with the arm down beside the body at every stance.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Pick this when you have wall access on an off day, or when you want the day to count without loading fingers hard. It's skill work — judge it by using less force, not by minutes.

setup: Any wall you can lap easily — autobelay is ideal, 5.9 to 5.10-.
Nothing at your limit. This is a skill day.
warmup: One easy lap, deliberately slow.

blocks.name: Economy laps
steps: 4–6 laps on terrain well below your limit.
OPEN HAND ONLY. No crimping, even where crimping would be easier.
No re-gripping and no matching. Grab it once, use it, move on.
Deliberately the loosest grip that still holds — actively try to slip, then back off a hair.
At every clip stance: full shakeout, hand completely OFF the hold, arm straight down by your side. 20 seconds.
Silent feet. If you hear your foot land, that rep didn't count.

cues: Shaking with the hand still on the hold does far less — arm down beside the body is worth about 22% more time to failure.
Judge this session by whether you can hold a hold with less force. Not by how many minutes you accumulated.

Cap continuous climbing at 15 minutes — past that this stops being a skill drill and becomes ARC, which is its own card now (ARC laps) and is graded as mileage rather than as a stimulus. Two different sessions; run one or the other, not fifteen minutes of both.
stopIf: You start crimping without deciding to — that's fatigue, and the drill is over.
log: Laps
Did you actually keep it open-handed, yes/no

outputs.label: Hard finger day?
outputs.hint: This is the answer the budget counts — not what the session was planned as. Two a week, three at a push, never two days running.

how.gist: Easy laps, open hand only, loosest grip that holds, silent feet.
steps: Pick terrain well below your limit.
Open hand only — no crimping, even where crimping is easier.
Grab each hold once. No re-gripping, no matching.
At every stance: hand fully off, arm down by your side, shake 20 seconds.
how.watch: If you hear your foot land, that lap didn't count.

dailyMenu.name: Antagonist + shoulders
dailyMenu.dose: Press-ups, external rotation, wrist extension, scap work. Zero finger loading. This absolutely counts as a day.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Pick this when your fingers need a genuine break but you still want the streak. Also the honest answer on a bad-sleep or high-stress day.

setup: Floor space. A band if you have one. No finger loading at all today.
warmup: Arm circles, 30s each direction.

blocks.name: Push / pull balance
steps: Press-ups: 3 × 10–15. Slow, full range, elbows tucked.
Band external rotation: 3 × 15 each arm, elbow pinned to your side.
Wrist extension: 3 × 20 each arm with a light weight or band — this is the one that protects your elbows.
Scapular pull-ups: 3 × 8. Hang, then shrug your shoulders DOWN without bending your arms.
Finger extension against a rubber band: 2 × 20.

cues: None of this should be hard. It's balance work, not a workout.
The wrist extension is the highest-value item here — climbers who skip it get elbow pain.
stopIf: Elbow pain — reduce range, don't push through.
log: Done, yes/no

how.gist: Ordinary press-ups, slow, elbows tucked close to your ribs.
steps: Hands under your shoulders, body in one straight line.
Lower over 2 seconds until your chest is near the floor.
Elbows stay close to your ribs, not flared out wide.
Press back up. 10–15 reps.
how.watch: Hips sagging or piking up. Squeeze your glutes for the whole set.
how.easier: Too hard? Put your hands on a chair or a stair.

how.gist: Elbow pinned to your ribs, rotate the forearm outward against a band.
steps: Stand side-on to the band, elbow tucked hard against your ribs.
Bend the elbow 90°, forearm across your belly.
Rotate the forearm out away from your body. The elbow never moves.
Return slowly. 15 reps each arm.
how.watch: If the elbow drifts off your ribs, the shoulder has stopped working.

how.gist: Forearm on your thigh, palm down, lift the weight with your wrist.
steps: Sit. Lay the forearm on your thigh, hand hanging off past the knee.
Palm facing DOWN, light weight or a band in the hand.
Lift the back of the hand up as far as it goes.
Lower slowly. 20 reps each arm.
how.watch: Only the hand moves. If the forearm lifts, the weight is too heavy.

how.gist: Hang with straight arms and shrug your shoulders DOWN. No bending.
steps: Hang from a jug, arms completely straight, shoulders relaxed up by your ears.
Without bending your elbows, pull the shoulders down away from your ears.
Your whole body rises an inch or two. That is the rep.
Lower back into the relaxed hang. 8 reps.
how.watch: Arms bending turns this into a pull-up. Keep them locked straight.

dailyMenu.tier: HARD — Monday, while you are fresh
dailyMenu.name: Max hangs
dailyMenu.dose: Three near-max 7-second hangs on the 20mm, three minutes apart, done completely fresh. Repeaters used to be bolted onto the end of this. They are their own card now, and the app offers them alongside.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Monday is where it belongs — it wants the freshest day of the week. If you missed Monday you can shift it later; the app will tell you which days are legal, and the only unbreakable part is that it cannot land the day after another hard finger day.

protocol.duration: 20 min including warm-up. Most of it is sitting down.
setup: Basement board. 20mm rung for the work, 25/30mm for warm-up.
Eyebolt + pulley rigged from the joist, harness on, counterweight bucket within reach.
Have your peak-force number written down. The load below is a percentage of it.
A towel to sit on. The three minutes between sets are sitting-down minutes.

Now that you have the Tindeq you can anchor this properly: measure a 6-second max pull PER HAND on the Port-A-Board, sum both hands, and work against that figure rather than against a remembered number. Run the Peak force test session when it is due.
warmup: 2 min: shake the arms out, wrist circles both directions, open and close the fists 20×.
Feet-on-floor hang on the big top rail, 30s. Rest 60s.
3 × 10s on the 25mm at roughly half your max, 60s rest between. Feet lightly assisting is fine.
1 × 7s on the 20mm at about 70%. Then rest 3 FULL minutes, sitting down.
Do not skip the 3 minutes. Skipping it turns your max test into an endurance test.

blocks.name: The work — protect the engine
steps: 3 sets × 7 seconds on the 20mm, two hands, half crimp. Three, not four — you still have repeaters after this.
3 minutes rest between sets. Sit down for it.
Half crimp means fingers bent to roughly 90° at the middle knuckle, thumb off the board.
Arms slightly bent, shoulders pulled DOWN and back. Never hang dead off the joints.
If you cannot hold a clean 7 seconds on set 2, stop here. That still counts, and it is the whole session — there is no block B to save yourself for any more.

cues: Breathe out during each hang. Almost everyone holds their breath and it costs them the last second.
Weight into the fingers, not the arms — you are not doing a pull-up.
Near-max INTENT is what the maintenance evidence cares about. A tired 85% hang is not a cheaper version of this session, it is a different one.
stopIf: Any sharp or pinpoint pain in a finger — not soreness, PAIN. Stop the session immediately.
Any pop, click, or twinge in a finger. Stop, ice, and take three days off finger loading.
You cannot hold a clean 7 seconds on set 2. The engine is not there today; do not chase it.

How the last rep felt, 1–5

Hang 7 seconds at your working load. Breathe out through it.
Sit down for 3 full minutes. Three sets.

dailyMenu.tier: HARD — after max hangs, or on its own
dailyMenu.name: Repeaters
dailyMenu.dose: Intermittent repeaters, 10s on / 6s off. The load is set by a COMPLETION CRITERION, not by a percentage of your hang max — expect to be taking weight OFF on 20mm.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Normally it rides along after max hangs on Monday, and the app offers it there. On its own it is a hard finger day in its own right and obeys the same spacing rule. Do not do it the day after max hangs to "finish Monday off" — that is two hard finger days back to back.

protocol.duration: 25 min cold. 20 if you have just done max hangs and are already warm.
setup: Coming straight off max hangs: you are already set up. Rest the 8 minutes and start.
Cold start: run the max-hang warm-up first, minus the final 7-second effort. You are not testing anything here.
20mm rung. Counterweight bucket and pulley within reach — on this session the pulley usually comes off the joist, not the harness.
Have last week's load to hand. That number, not a percentage, is what you progress.
warmup: Straight off max hangs: nothing extra. The 8-minute rest IS the transition.
Cold: 2 min shaking out, wrist circles, open and close the fists 20×.
Feet-on hang on the big top rail, 30s. Rest 60s.
3 × 10s on the 25mm at roughly half max, 60s between. Feet lightly assisting is fine.
Rest 3 full minutes before set 1.

blocks.name: The work — set the load by completion, not by percentage
steps: REST 8 FULL MINUTES after your last max hang. Not 3. The source protocol used 8 minutes between sets and it matters.

Set the load so you can complete 8–12 reps with the last one clean. On 20mm that will almost certainly mean COUNTERWEIGHT — taking weight off with the pulley, not adding it. That is correct and expected, not a sign you are weak.
10 seconds on, 6 seconds off. Hands OFF the board between reps, arms by your sides.
END THE SET when your force visibly drops or your fingers roll open from half crimp — not at a rep count.
2 sets, 8 minutes between them.
Write down the load you actually used. Add a little only when you can finish both sets cleanly at 12 reps.

cues: The load is right when set 1 feels manageable and set 2 is genuinely hard by rep 8.
If you are ADDING weight on a 20mm edge here, the load is almost certainly too high.
Breathe out through each rep. Hands all the way off between them — a resting fingertip is not a rest.
stopIf: Any sharp or pinpoint pain in a finger — not soreness, PAIN. Stop the session immediately.
You can't complete 6 reps in set 1: the load is too high. Drop it 10% and write that down.
Any pop, click, or twinge in a finger. Stop, ice, and take three days off finger loading.

outputs.label: Hard finger day?
outputs.hint: This is the answer the budget counts — not what the session was planned as. Two a week, three at a push, never two days running.

how.gist: 10 seconds on, 6 off, hands right off between reps. Expect counterweight.
steps: Rest 8 full minutes after the last max hang. Not 3.
Set the load so rep 8–12 is the last clean one — on 20 mm that means taking weight OFF.
Hang 10 seconds, then hands completely off the board for 6, arms by your sides.
End the set when force drops or your fingers roll open — not at a rep count.
how.watch: Adding weight on a 20 mm edge here almost always means the load is too high.

dailyMenu.tier: TEST — every 3 weeks, instead of max hangs
dailyMenu.name: Peak force test
dailyMenu.dose: Three maximal 5-second pulls per hand on the Port-A-Board 20mm with the Tindeq, 3 minutes between every attempt. Best of three per hand. It replaces max hangs on the day you run it — measured properly, it IS the max hang.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Monday, in place of max hangs, no more often than every 3 weeks and never within 48h of a hard finger day. Repeaters can still ride along after it — the app offers them. Do not run it on the same day as the 4-min critical-force test unless you have a clear 10 minutes between; better still, give that one its own day.

protocol.duration: 20–25 min. Most of it is rest, and the rest is the test.
setup: Tindeq Progressor 200, Port-A-Board on its rated cord, a sling or foot loop to anchor to the floor, a carabiner.
Anchor the gauge to the floor with a sling under your foot. Board clipped to the other end.
Stand tall, arm at your side, elbow slightly bent. SAME body position every time — write down where your feet are.
Same edge, same grip, same time of day. Any change starts a new series and makes the old one worthless.
warmup: 3 progressively harder pulls at roughly 50%, 70%, 85%, one minute between.
Rest 3 full minutes before the first real attempt.
Do not skip the 3 minutes. Under-resting turns a strength test into an endurance test.

blocks.name: A · Left hand — best of three
steps: 20mm edge, half crimp, ONE hand. Pull to max over about 2 seconds and hold for 5.
3 attempts, 3 minutes rest between every one.
Record the best of the three, not the average.
If attempt 3 is well below attempt 1, you are fatigued rather than weak — note it and do not add a fourth.

blocks.name: B · Right hand — best of three
steps: Same rig, same body position, same 3 minutes between attempts.
3 attempts. Best of three.
Left/right asymmetry over about 10% is worth noting. Under that is noise — do not train around it.
Saving this session writes the result onto the Peak force chart on the Testing tab. You do not have to log it twice.

cues: Same body position every single time. Arm position materially changes measured finger force; a new setup is a new series.
Never compare this number to a hang number. Different instruments, no conversion exists.
A change under about 6% is inside the noise band — for a 50 kg pull that is 3 kg.

Any pop, click, or twinge. Stop, ice, three days off finger loading.
Elbow pain that builds across attempts.

outputs.label: Hard finger day?
outputs.hint: This is the answer the budget counts — not what the session was planned as. Two a week, three at a push, never two days running.

how.gist: Three maximal 5-second pulls, left hand, three minutes apart.
steps: Sling under your foot, gauge on the floor, board at the other end of the cord.
Stand tall, arm straight down at your side, elbow just off locked. Same spot every time.
Build to max over about 2 seconds, then hold everything you have for 5.
Sit down for 3 full minutes. Three attempts, and keep the best.
how.watch: Leaning back or bending the elbow adds your body to the number and ruins the series.

how.gist: Same again, right hand. Same rig, same rests, best of three.
steps: Do not change the setup between hands — the comparison is the point.
Build to max over 2 seconds, hold for 5.
3 minutes between attempts, sitting down.
Three attempts, best of three. Then stop, whatever the number said.
how.watch: Chasing a fourth attempt when three were flat measures your stubbornness, not your fingers.

dailyMenu.tier: TEST — every 4–5 weeks, instead of max hangs
dailyMenu.name: MVC-7 test
dailyMenu.dose: Work up in 5 lb steps to the heaviest 7-second hang you can hold CLEAN on the 20mm, two hands, half crimp. Five attempts maximum, five minutes between every one. The heaviest clean 7 seconds is the number, and every percentage in this plan is a percentage of it.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: In place of max hangs, no more often than every 4–5 weeks — measured properly this IS the max hang. Repeaters can still ride along afterwards: give it 8 full minutes and expect the load to read low, because you just went to failure five times. Never the day after a hard finger day, and never on split or thin skin.

protocol.duration: 40–50 min, and most of it is sitting on the floor. The rests are the test — under-resting is the classic way to measure yourself low.
setup: Basement board, 20mm rung for the work, 25/30mm for the warm-up. Dip belt if you have it on, harness if not.
Lay the plates out as a ladder BEFORE you start: your opener, then +5, +5, +5, +5. Deciding what to add mid-test burns a rest period.
Pulley and bucket still rigged — the warm-up ramp takes weight OFF, the attempts put weight ON.
Weigh yourself and log it. This test produces a TOTAL load, and total load is you plus the iron.
A towel to sit on and a timer. Five minutes between attempts, sitting down, is not optional.
warmup: 10 min easy movement first: shake the arms out, wrist circles both ways, open and close the fists 20×.
Feet-on-floor hang on the big top rail, 30s. Rest 60s.
3 × 10s on the 25mm at roughly half effort, 60s between. Feet lightly assisting is fine.
Ramp on the 20mm: 7s at about 50%, then 70%, then 85% of what you expect to hold, 2 min between. The first two come off the pulley; the last is near bodyweight.
Then sit down for 5 FULL minutes before attempt 1. This is the rest that decides whether the number is honest.

blocks.name: The ladder — heaviest clean 7 seconds
steps: Attempt 1: load to about what you expect to hold. You are not trying to fail here, you are calibrating the ladder.
Add 5 lb and go again. Five attempts total, five minutes sitting down between every one.
It only counts as CLEAN if all seven seconds were clean: half crimp held, fingers never rolling open, shoulders never sagging into the joint.
Log every attempt — the weight AND the seconds you actually held. A 4-second failure at 60 lb is data, not a wasted set.
The heaviest load you held clean for a full 7 seconds is the result. Stop there. Do not chase a sixth attempt.

cues: Same edge, same grip, same 7 seconds every time you run this. Change one of them and the series starts over from scratch.
Half crimp means middle knuckles at roughly 90°, thumb off the board. A grip that drifts open produces a bigger number that means nothing.
Weight into the fingers, not the arms. Breathe out through the hang — holding your breath costs most people the last second.
A change smaller than about 6% — is inside the noise band. Maintenance is a win during this block; you are not trying to add strength here.
stopIf: Any sharp or pinpoint pain in a finger — not soreness, PAIN. Stop the session immediately.
Any pop, click or twinge in a finger. Stop, ice, three days off finger loading.
Two attempts running where you cannot hold a clean 7 seconds. The engine is not there today, and the last clean attempt is your number.
Skin splitting or a hot spot forming. A test run on torn skin measures your skin.

outputs.label: Hard finger day?
outputs.hint: This is the answer the budget counts — not what the session was planned as. Two a week, three at a push, never two days running.

how.gist: Work up in 5 lb steps to the heaviest clean 7-second hang.
steps: 20 mm rung, both hands, half crimp — middle knuckles about 90°, thumb off.
Arms slightly bent, shoulders pulled DOWN and back. Never dangle in the joint.
Hang 7 seconds. Clean means the grip never opened and the shoulders never sagged.
Add 5 lb, sit down for 5 full minutes, go again. Five attempts maximum.
Log the weight and the seconds you actually held, every attempt.
how.watch: Under-resting is how you measure yourself weak. Five minutes between attempts, sitting down, every single time.
how.easier: Can't hold a clean 7s on attempt 1? Take weight off with the pulley and ladder up from there — the number is still the number.

evidence.transfer: NO transfer is claimed and none is demonstrated. This session does not train anything — it is a measurement, and the reason it exists is that every load in this plan is written as a percentage of it. Without a logged MVC-7 the app cannot turn '95% of max' into pounds on the belt, and 'roughly what I did last time' is not a training load. The one claim being made is narrow: a weighted hang on a standard edge, at a fixed duration and grip, is a reliable enough number to compare against itself month to month.
evidence.summary: Reliability of maximal isometric finger-strength testing: Pérez-Cordero et al. 2025, systematic review of 15 studies / 747 climbers, found a median ICC of 0.86, highest (>0.90) on standardised 20–23 mm edges with a fixed half crimp — which is exactly this protocol, and is why the edge, grip and hang length are pinned. HONEST CAVEAT, because this plan states its own weak spots: the ±6% noise band quoted on this test is borrowed from McClean et al. 2023 (n=13), where a 5.6% CV was measured for PEAK FORCE ON A LOAD CELL, not for a weighted hang. Nobody has published a test-retest CV for a harness-loaded 7-second hang, and a hang carries sources of variation a block pull does not — harness position, foot-off timing, how the plates swing. Treat 6% as the optimistic floor on the noise, not a measured value. The practical consequence: 5 lb steps are finer than this test can actually resolve (5 lb is about 2% of a typical total load), so the ladder's job is to find the boundary, not to claim precision it does not have.

dailyMenu.name: Crimp crawls
dailyMenu.dose: Feet on the stairs, hands crawling across the rungs, changing hold every 3–5 seconds. TWO sets of three minutes, then one all-out set — crawl until you come off, with the clock counting up, so how long you lasted is the number the session progresses on. Draws are hung round the board now: clip them as you pass. You get pumped on purpose and keep going, shaking out on the big rail when it peaks. Raise your feet a stair to make it harder — the stair number IS the load.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Any day that is not a hard finger day and is not the day after one. It is deliberately NOT a rest-day session: the fingers see low peak force, but the forearms work for the whole set. Easy on the tissue, hard on the system.

setup: Basement board. Big top rail or the jugs for shake-outs, 25mm and 20mm rungs for the crawling.
Quickdraws hung round the board, at the reaches you actually clip from. Clipping while pumped is why they are there — a clip is part of the crawl now, not an extra.
The stairs in front of the board. Stair 1 is the lowest your feet go; every stair up moves more of you onto your fingers.
Start on the stair you finished on last time — it is in your log. If there is no log yet, start on stair 1.
A clock you can see. You are watching minutes, not counting reps.
No load cell, no harness, no counterweight. Your feet are the dial.
warmup: 2 min: shake the arms out, wrist circles both directions, open and close the fists 20×.
60s crawl on the big top rail only, feet flat on the floor, clipping one draw as you pass it. This should feel like nothing — it is the rehearsal for the clip, not the clip that counts.
Rest 2 min. Then one 30s crawl on the rungs, feet one stair BELOW your working stair.
Rest 3 min sitting down, then start set 1.

blocks.name: A · The crawls — two sets of three minutes, hands never still
steps: Feet on your working stair, hands on the rungs. Move ONE hand every 3–5 seconds and keep moving for the whole three minutes.

Half crimp or open hand on the 20–25mm rungs, thumb off. Do not full crimp. The pump will degrade your grip long before the set ends, and a full crimp that collapses is the position this session must not put you in.

Clip a draw when you pass one — hand off the rung, clip, back on, keep crawling. Do not stop the clock for it and do not count them; the checkbox in the log is all the record it needs. Clipping while pumped is the thing that actually goes on lead, and this is the only session that drills it.
When the pump peaks, move both hands to the big rail for 10–15 seconds and shake one arm at a time, then go back to the rungs. The shake-out is part of the set, not a break from it.
INTENSITY: you should finish three minutes pumped and still holding on. Falling off before two minutes means drop a stair. Finishing barely pumped means go up a stair next time.
5 minutes rest between sets, sitting down. TWO sets here — the third one is block B, and it is a different set.

blocks.name: B · The all-out set — one set, everything left, on the clock
steps: 5 minutes sitting down after set 2, the same rest as between the others. Same stair, same rungs — nothing changes but the instruction.

Crawl until you come off. No target and no pacing: hands moving every 3–5 seconds, shake-outs on the big rail when you need them, draws clipped as you pass, and keep going until your fingers actually open.

The clock counts UP on this one. Workout mode starts it with the set and writes the seconds into the log when you tap done, so the only thing you have to remember is which stair you were on. Logging it by hand instead: read the time off your own timer and type it in.

ONE set. Crawling to failure, resting as long as you lasted and repeating until you cannot is the tempting version, but it has no floor, and without one it turns a 22-minute session into a 50-minute one you pay for on Thursday. One all-out set is the version that fits the week.

EXPECT 2–5 minutes. Under 90 seconds on your working stair means either the two sets before it were too hard or the stair is too high — drop a stair next time rather than fighting this one. Past 6 minutes and the stair is too low to be worth an all-out set.
HONEST GRADING: block A sits in the intensity band Devise 2022 actually tested. This does not. Nobody has trained an all-out finisher on a moving hang and measured anything, either way.

cues: Keep the feet quiet. If you are pushing hard through your legs to survive, the stair is too high and your fingers are not doing the work.
Shoulders down and back for the whole set. Three minutes of dead-hanging shoulders is how the elbows start talking.
Breathe. The pump is the point; holding your breath through it is not.
Clip like you are on the sharp end — reach, clip, back on the rung. A clip you rush at home is a clip you fumble on the rock.
The stair is the load — log it every time, or the session has no progression at all. The all-out set's seconds are the other half of that: same stair, longer set, is the whole signal.
This is the one session where the target weakness is trained directly: staying on when pumped, and recovering without coming off.
stopIf: Any sharp or pinpoint pain in a finger — not soreness, PAIN. Stop the session immediately.
Any pop, click, or twinge. Stop, ice, and take three days off finger loading.
Medial or lateral elbow pain that builds across the sets. Come off the stair, not through it.

Your fingers start rolling open involuntarily on the BIG rail. In the three-minute sets that is past useful and into sloppy — end the set. In the all-out set it IS the end of the set, so come off rather than fighting the rail.
Skin reading 4/5 before you start. Wood plus three minutes of moving hands is the most skin-hungry thing in the menu.

outputs.label: Hard finger day?
outputs.hint: This is the answer the budget counts — not what the session was planned as. Two a week, three at a push, never two days running.

how.gist: Feet on a stair, hands moving across the rungs for three minutes.
steps: Feet on your working stair, both hands on the rungs, shoulders down and back.
Move one hand to a new rung every 3–5 seconds. Never let both hands settle.
Clip a draw as you pass it — one hand off, clip, back on, keep crawling.
When the pump peaks, both hands to the big rail, shake one arm at a time, then carry on.
Keep going for the full three minutes. Sit down for five. Two of these, then the all-out set.
how.watch: Feet pushing hard to survive means the stair is too high — your legs are doing the session.
how.easier: Drop a stair, or spend more of the set on the 25mm rungs and the big rail.

how.gist: Same stair, same rungs — crawl until you come off, and the clock counts up.
steps: Five minutes sitting down first, the same rest as between the three-minute sets.
Same stair. Start the clock, get on, and crawl exactly as before — hands moving, draws clipped, shake-outs on the big rail.
No target. Keep going until your fingers open on their own, then come off.
Tap done and the seconds you lasted are written into the log. That number is the session's progress.
One set. Then you are finished — no second attempt, however good it felt.
how.watch: Under 90 seconds means the stair is too high for a set with nothing held back. Drop one next time.
how.easier: Drop a stair, or take the all-out set on the 25mm rungs and keep the 20s for the three-minute sets.

evidence.transfer: ASSUMED, not demonstrated. What is demonstrated is that intermittent sub-maximal finger loading improves how long you can hold a given force and how much force you keep once exhausted: Devise et al. 2022 (n=54 advanced/elite, 4 weeks, 2 sessions/week) moved "stamina" from 33% to 54% and "endurance" from 66% to 79% in the 60%-of-max group, with maximal strength unchanged (+0.7%, n.s.). That is the exact signature this block wants — endurance moving while max holds. But nobody has trained the feet-on moving-hang version and measured anything at all. The bet is that a drill in the same intensity band with far longer time under tension buys the same adaptation, plus the skill of continuing to climb while pumped. The all-out third set (block B) is a further step away from the evidence and is labelled as such on the block: a set taken to failure is a different stimulus from the controlled band Devise tested, nobody has trialled it, and it is in the session for the practice of holding on while pumped rather than because a study asked for it. Same for the draws — clipping mid-crawl is skill rehearsal, costs the fingers nothing extra, and is claimed as nothing more.
evidence.summary: The drill is Eric Hörst's "moving hangs" (Conditioning for Climbers, 2008) — feet supported, hands changing hold every 3–5 seconds, 5–10 min per set. It is expert consensus with no trial behind it. With the feet supported the fingers carry roughly 30–70% of bodyweight depending on how far back the feet are, which is why the stair is the load dial and why this is not a hard finger exposure: peak force per finger is far below a max hang, so pulley stress is low. Two honest limits. FIRST, this is not ARC and must not be sold as capillarisation — this plan already grades that claim REFUTED (see the Why tab): climbers do show real microvascular adaptation (Thompson 2015, capillary filtration capacity), but no trial has ever shown easy continuous climbing causes it, and the largest meta-analysis found low-intensity work produced the smallest capillary gains and none at all in trained subjects. What justifies this session is the INTENSITY band Devise tested, not the volume. SECOND, "good for recovering" is only half true. Peak finger force is low, so it is kind to the tissue and does not spend a hard finger exposure. It is still genuinely fatiguing to the forearm, so it does not belong the day after a hard session and it is not a rest day. Easy on the tissue, hard on the system.
sources: Devise, Lechaptois, Berton & Vigouroux 2022, Front Sports Act Living 4:862782 (n=54, RCT)
Hörst, Conditioning for Climbers, 2008 (expert consensus, no trial)
Thompson et al. 2015, Eur J Sport Sci (capillary filtration capacity in climbers)
Fryer et al. 2015 (forearm reoxygenation and climbing ability)

dailyMenu.name: Gym: board
dailyMenu.dose: Board intervals — three problems linked back to back, four times, 4:00 between. Real power endurance, which is what this session used to claim and was not. Your other hard exposure — normally Thursday, 72h clear of Monday, and never the day after another hard finger day. The doubled lead laps are their own session on the same night, not part of this one.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Only on Thursday (Wednesday fallback). If you miss the gym entirely this week, THIS is when Saturday becomes your second hard session instead. The laps are a separate card — dropping the board does not drop them. From week 7 the 4×4 takes over as the higher-density version of the same stimulus; the two are the same job and never go on one day.

setup: Tension Board at this week's angle — check the Plan tab for which. Cap it at 30°: a middle angle loads the flexors for the whole interval, where 40°+ adds limit-crimp spikes, and spikes taken while fatigued are the documented acute pulley mechanism.

Pick THREE problems, three full grades below your limit, 8–12 hand moves each. Three below, not two — you climb them linked, so each one has to still be clean on move 30. Two grades below is the number for single rested ascents, which is what this session used to be.
Write the three down before you start. Choosing them while pumped is how the session quietly gets easier.
A timer you can hear, running the whole session. Untimed chalking and beta talk is the single most common way this workout stops being this workout.
Same test boulder available if it's a test week.
warmup: This is the non-negotiable part. An interval goes from cold to sustained near-limit flexor load inside two minutes.
10 min easy movement — traverse, easy boulders, get genuinely warm before you touch the board.
The Pre-Session Dynamic Warm-Up from the add-ons, in full.
3–4 board problems climbing up in difficulty, finishing one grade below your interval problems.
5 min rest before interval 1. Total warm-up 25–30 minutes. If you do not have time for the warm-up, you do not have time for the intervals — climb easy board volume instead and say so in the log.

blocks.name: A · Board intervals
steps: 1. One interval = your three problems climbed back to back. Step off only long enough to walk to the next start — about 10 seconds, and it is a transition, not a rest.

2. That is 90–120 seconds of continuous climbing, which is roughly what an outdoor 5.12a asks of you between one rest and the next. The pump inside a single interval IS the stimulus; that is the part the old version of this session did not have.

3. Rest 4:00 between intervals. Not 2–3. An intermediate climber's forearm reoxygenation half-time is about 83 s where an elite climber's is 8 (Fryer 2015), so an intermediate is 63% recovered at 2 minutes, 78% at 3 and 87% at 4. Below 4:00 the later intervals are low-quality flailing at maximum injury exposure.
4. FOUR intervals — twelve ascents — unless the Plan tab says otherwise for this week. Then stop. Do not run a fifth because you feel good.

5. During every rest: arms DOWN and shaken loose beside your body. Not on your knees, not holding your phone. That position alone increased intermittent test time by 22% and reoxygenation rate by 32% versus leaving the hand on the hold (Baláš 2016). Recovering at a rest is the exact skill the trip needs and this is where you drill it.

6. TARGET: one fall or fewer across all four intervals. Zero falls with the last interval feeling like the first means it is too easy — add an interval or a grade next week, never less rest. Two falls inside a single interval means abort that interval.

7. THE NUMBER THAT SAYS WHETHER THE DOSE WAS RIGHT: your last interval should take within 10–15% of the time your first one did. Workout mode logs each interval's length off the clock, so you do not have to time it yourself. If interval 4 took 40% longer, the dose was wrong, and you write that down rather than repeating it.

blocks.name: B · Finish
steps: One easy lap to cool down.
Do NOT add limit bouldering at the end because you feel good. This session is already hard exposure #2.
Doubled lead laps are their own card tonight, and they still happen — three doubles as normal, two on any week block A runs five intervals. Log them separately; they are not a sub-block of this.

SAY THE TRADE OUT LOUD so it stays deliberate: you have given up low-density board volume, which is what fed the week-9 repeated-ascent retest, and bought a power-endurance stimulus Thursday did not previously contain. The retest is still run at the same angle on the same boulder, so it still compares — but expect the volume-driven part of that number to move less than it would have.

cues: 'Density, not difficulty.' The stimulus is three problems with nothing between them. Making the problems harder is a different workout.
'Fail from pump, not from power.' If you cannot generate force on move three of a fresh interval, the problems are too hard and you are accidentally doing a strength session.
'The timer decides, not you.' Rest creep — chalking, brushing, talking beta — is the most common and least noticed way this stops working.
This is one of at most three hard finger days this week, and the week normally plans for two. Treat it that way — don't casually add a bouldering session on top.
If you're wrecked from Monday, cut to three intervals rather than skipping the day. Cut intervals, never the 4:00.
stopIf: Any sharp or localised finger pain, especially at the base of a finger — stop mid-interval, do not finish it.
Any audible pop or click at a finger base. Session over. That is a pulley.
You are falling off from fatigue rather than difficulty. Twelve sloppy ascents on board wood is a skin injury with a finger injury attached.
Two falls inside a single interval — the problems are wrong, stop rather than pushing through.
Medial elbow ache developing mid-session. High-volume flexor work drives it.
A flapper or a hot spot. Skin binds before muscle does on wood, and climbing the last intervals on compromised skin means climbing them with unreliable grip.
log: Intervals completed, and how long each one took
Rest you actually took between intervals, not the rest you intended
Board angle

OPTIONAL, and worth it on a session you want to look back at: 'log each problem' opens a line per problem in each interval — its grade, what kind of climbing it was, and whether you fell on it. That is the session's own target made countable, since 'one fall or fewer across all four intervals' is a number you cannot check from memory a week later. It is per interval on purpose: the three problems are the same all night, but the fall that matters happened in interval 3, not interval 1.

how.gist: Three easy problems climbed back to back. That is one interval.
steps: Pick 3 problems about 3 grades below your limit, at this week's angle.
Climb all three back to back — step off only to walk to the next start.
Rest 4:00 between intervals. Never less: at 3:00 you are only 78% recovered.
Arms down and shaken loose the whole rest. That is the drill, not a break.
Four intervals, then stop. One fall or fewer across all of them.
how.watch: A 4:00 rest that drifts to 6:00 is the usual way this stops working. Start on the beep.

evidence.transfer: The PROTOCOL CLASS has a randomised trial behind it; these specific numbers do not. Medernach 2015 trained interval bouldering against conventional bouldering and moved a climbing endurance outcome, which is more than can be said for the 4×4's famous parameters or for what this session used to be. But the trial used highly-advanced male boulderers, ran four weeks, and measured climbing time to exhaustion — not redpoint grade, not a sustained 5.12a, and not on an intermediate route climber. The three-problem link, the four intervals and the 4:00 rest are DERIVED here rather than tested: the work bout from the 2–7 minute duration Watts measured for a hard route ascent, the rest from Fryer's reoxygenation half-time, the volume from wanting a build-phase dose below the week-7 4×4's sixteen ascents. Two 2024 RCTs are the honest counterweight — Saeterbakken (n=31) moved finger strength (+11.5% vs +5.3%, p=0.021) with bouldering performance unchanged (p=0.39), and Langer (n=26) found no between-group difference at all after five weeks of on-the-wall board intervals. So: a defensible stimulus in the right energy system, replacing a block that was in no energy system in particular, with parameters that are reasoned rather than demonstrated.
evidence.summary: WHAT THIS REPLACED, AND WHY. Until 2026-08-13 block A was '8–10 problems 2 grades below limit, rest 2–3 minutes', labelled power endurance. It was not power endurance by any definition — at 2–3 minutes between single 25–35 second problems, fatigue never accumulates. The plan already knew: the 4×4 card's own evidence block said so in writing and the fix was never applied here. THE DIRECT EVIDENCE: Medernach, Kleinöder & Lötzerich (2015, Sports Technology 8:76–82) randomised 24 highly-advanced male boulderers to 4 weeks of interval bouldering (n=12) or conventional bouldering (n=12), 3 × 150 min/wk. Climbing time to exhaustion improved +36.2 ± 14.1 s (p<0.001) in the interval group versus +6.1 ± 19.3 s (p=0.298) in controls, with intermittent finger-hang time improving only in the interval group. Stien et al. (2023, Biology of Sport) meta-analysed 11 studies / 225 climbers and concluded interval-style bouldering 'may' improve climbing, but could not meta-analyse climbing-performance outcomes at all — median PEDro 6/10, no study blinded assessors. THE ENERGY SYSTEM: this is not lactate tolerance. Maciejczyk et al. (2022, Front Physiol, n=13) measured intermittent climbing of comparable duration at 59.9% aerobic / 12.9% anaerobic-lactic / 27.2% alactic, and Watts (2004, Eur J Appl Physiol) characterised a hard route ascent as a 2–7 minute effort at ~20–25 ml/kg/min. The target is oxidative capacity and reoxygenation between grips. THE REST LENGTH: Fryer et al. (2015, JSCR 29(6):1633–1639, n=44 across control/intermediate/advanced/elite) measured forearm reoxygenation half-time on INTERMITTENT contractions at 40% MVC in the flexor digitorum profundus at 8 s for elites, 83 s for intermediates and 93 s for non-climbing controls; on sustained contractions the intermediate figure was 47 s. Assuming exponential recovery from the 83 s intermittent figure puts an intermediate climber at 63% recovered at 2:00, 78% at 3:00, 87% at 4:00 and 92% at 5:00. NOTE A CORRECTED CITATION: this card previously read '~47–93s for intermediates versus ~8s for elites'. The 93 s is the CONTROL group's intermittent value, not an intermediate one; the range conflated two groups. Verified against the full text 2026-08-13. THE SHAKEOUT: the best-evidenced single instruction in the session. Baláš et al. (2016) found recovering with the forearm shaken beside the body increased intermittent test time by 22% and reoxygenation rate by 32% versus leaving the hand on the hold.

dailyMenu.name: Limit bouldering

dailyMenu.name: Walk the Rest
dailyMenu.dose: After every hard lead lap or redpoint burn: walk continuously at a brisk conversational pace (~6 km/h / 3.7 mph) for the first 3–4 min of the rest, hands empty — no shaking out, no easy climbing, no hanging on jugs.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Use this on Thursday (gym: doubled lead laps) and on every outdoor day between October burns. It is not a home session — it is a rule for what the athlete does with their hands and legs during the rest interval the athlete is already taking. It costs zero extra training load, so it never competes with anything else in the menu.

evidence.transfer: This is the closest thing in the whole aerobic domain to DEMONSTRATED transfer, and it is still only partial. What is demonstrated: in climbers, filling the rest interval with whole-body walking preserves repeat finger-flexor performance better than filling it with easy climbing or hanging, and lowers blood lactate and RPE between real climbing bouts. What is NOT demonstrated: that this makes anyone redpoint a harder grade, and that being aerobically FITTER makes the walk work better. Note the important logical point — this candidate requires no aerobic training at all. It is a behaviour change during rests, not a fitness adaptation. It is in this domain only because the effective modality happens to be low-intensity whole-body movement.
evidence.summary: Two controlled crossover studies in climbers, both with a climbing-relevant outcome. Krupková, Tufano & Baláš (2024, Frontiers in Sports and Active Living), n=17 male sport climbers (IRCRA 10–25), randomized crossover: three exhaustive intermittent isometric finger-flexor tests at 60% MVC, each separated by 22 min of assigned active recovery (treadmill walking at 6 km/h, 60–65% HRmax; easy climbing on a motorized wall ~IRCRA 3; or intermittent hanging at 50% critical force). Impulse fell −18.4% from trial 1 to trial 3 after walking versus −27.2% after hanging and −29.5% after easy climbing; trial-3 impulse was 21,253±5,650 N·s after walking vs 18,618±5,174 (hanging) and 18,508±4,435 (climbing). Authors' conclusion: 'using the same muscle group for AR should be avoided between exhaustive isometric contractions.' Draper, Bird, Coleman & Hodgson (2006, J Sports Sci Med 5:97–105), n=10 male

setup: A clear ~20–30 m loop: a gym hallway, the perimeter of the bouldering area, or the flat ground at the base of the crag.

blocks.name: The work
steps: 1. Lower off / drop off. Untie or unclip, take your shoes off, and start walking within about 20 seconds. Do not sit down first — sitting down is the habit this drill is replacing.

2. Walk continuously for 3–4 minutes at a brisk but easy pace: roughly 6 km/h (3.7 mph), the speed you'd walk if you were mildly late for something. You should be able to talk in full sentences but not want to sing. In the trial this corresponded to about 60–65% of maximum heart rate.

3. Let your arms hang and swing naturally at your sides. Hands stay EMPTY and relaxed. Specifically do not: shake out, do G-Tox arm-raises, hang off a jug, traverse the warm-up wall, or brush holds on your project.

4. Common error #1: 'staying warm' by pulling on easy terrain between burns. In the one controlled trial that tested this directly, easy climbing was the WORST of the three recovery modes — worse than doing nothing sport-specific at all. If you feel the urge to touch the wall, walk another lap instead.
5. Common error #2: walking too hard. This is not a cardio session. If you're breathing through your mouth or your legs feel it, slow down — you still have to climb.
6. After the 3–4 min walk, stop and rest quietly (stand or sit) for the remainder of the interval. Target total rest: ~5 min between lead laps, 15–25 min between genuine redpoint burns.
7. If you're swapping burns with a partner, take your walk in the FIRST 4 min of your rest, then go belay. Belaying is standing, not walking, and it doesn't count.
8. Repeat identically after every burn, including the last one of the day.

dailyMenu.name: Load-Cell Calibration Day
dailyMenu.dose: Once per 4-6 week block, on Monday INSTEAD of max hangs: 3 x per-arm MVC on the Port-A-Board's 20mm edge (3 min rest), then one 4-min all-out critical-force test (24 x 7s pull / 3s rest) on the dominant arm; record per-arm max, asymmetry %, CF, W', and CFmin — then set every sub-threshold dose for the next block as an absolute kg number.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Pick this over Monday's max hangs on the first Monday of a new block, and again ~6 weeks later (so: early August now that the Tindeq is here, mid-September, and optionally a final check ~2 weeks before the October trip). Never as an extra day — the 4-min all-out test IS a maximal finger exposure and must consume one of the two weekly slots.

evidence.transfer: NO transfer is claimed and none is demonstrated. This session does not train anything — it is a measurement that makes the sessions the athlete is already doing correctly dosed. The only transfer evidence in play is cross-sectional: CF/bodyweight correlates with sport-climbing grade (Giles 2021, n=129), which is an association, not proof that raising CF raises grade. No trial has shown that dosing sub-threshold work against a measured critical force produces better outcomes than guessing a %MVC. The specific claim I will defend is narrower and solid: %MVC does not map onto a metabolic intensity domain, whereas critical force does by definition, so 'sub-threshold' becomes a measured boundary instead of a coaching guess.
evidence.summary: The measurement tools are well validated; the training claim being made here is only 'dose it correctly.' Tindeq-class force sensors: validity ICC 0.99 against a laboratory force plate, between-day reliability ICC 0.95 (rung pull) and 0.98 (lock-off), n=25 climbers (Front Sports Act Living 2022). A systematic review of 15 studies / 747 climbers (Pérez-Cordero 2025) found median ICC 0.86 for maximal isometric finger strength, highest (>0.90) on standardised 20-23 mm edges with a fixed half crimp. Critical force: Giles et al. 2021 (IJSPP, n=129) — CF/body mass explained 61% of sport and 26% of bouldering performance; W'/body mass 7% and 34%; combined model 66% and 44%. Fryer et al. 2019 found CF sat at 425.7 ± 82.8 N, i.e. 41.0 ± 6.2% of MVC. LIMITATIONS, stated plainly: McClean et al. 2023 (n=13) measured test-retest of the 4-min all-out test at ICC 0.848 with a CV of 21.0% for end-test force, and ICC 0.820 / CV 13.2% for the impulse above it — so a single critical-force number carries far more noise than a max pull does, and only a trend across several tests means anything. Baláš et al. 2024 (n=12) then showed the reported CF overestimates the genuinely sustainable intensity: at CF itself only 1 of 12 completed a 720 s trial (mean time to failure 440 ± 140 s), rising to 38% at CF−2 kg, 69% at CF−4 kg and 92% at CF−6 kg. Both findings are why the working ceiling here is deliberately conservative and why retesting is capped at every 4–6 weeks.

setup: Tindeq Progressor 200 + Frictitious Port-A-Board, both of which you own. Phone with the Tindeq Progressor app, which has built-in Peak Force, Repeaters and Critical Force (with W') test modes.

Anchor option A (no drilling): a 1.2 m loop of tubular webbing or an old sling. Stand on the loop with BOTH feet, shoulder-width, so the loop is pinned under your midfoot. Clip the Tindeq into the top of the loop with a carabiner, then clip the Port-A-Board's rated cord to the Tindeq's other end. Adjust webbing length so that when you stand tall with the arm hanging straight down at your side, the block sits in your hand with a slight pre-tension and about 2-3 cm of slack removed.

Anchor option B (permanent): lag an eye bolt into the base plate / bottom of a joist near the floor and clip the Tindeq to that instead. Only do this if you can get the eye bolt into solid timber, not drywall.
Chalk. A timer is not needed — the app cues the intervals with sound.
Write your setup down on paper the first time: webbing length, standing vs seated, elbow angle, which edge face of the block, thumb on or off. You will reuse this exact setup forever.
warmup: 5 min general: brisk walk / stair climb / arm swings until hands are warm and pink. Cold fingers read low.
Wrist circles x10 each direction, then 20 slow finger flexion-extension reps against a rubber band.
On the block, 5-second pulls at roughly 20%, then 40%, then 60%, then 80% of what you think your max is, 60 s rest between. Watch the number on screen so you learn what each level feels like.

blocks.name: The work
steps: 1. PER-ARM MAX (MVC). Open the app's Peak Force / Max Pull test. Stand tall on the webbing loop, arm straight down at your side, shoulder relaxed and packed (not shrugged), wrist straight (neither bent toward the thumb nor toward the pinky), four fingers on the 20 mm face of the block in a half crimp — first knuckles bent, second knuckles at roughly 90 degrees, thumb off the block. Build force smoothly over ~2 seconds, hold maximum for ~3 seconds, then release smoothly. Do NOT jerk.
2. Rest 3 full minutes. Repeat on the other arm. Alternate arms until you have 3 attempts per arm (6 pulls total, ~15 min). Take the single best value for each arm.

3. COMPUTE ASYMMETRY. Asymmetry % = (stronger arm - weaker arm) / stronger arm x 100. Also record each arm as % of bodyweight, using your most recently logged bodyweight rather than a remembered one. For reference, Lattice's proprietary one-arm 20 mm dataset places V6 around 61% of bodyweight and V7 around 67% — that is coach data, not a peer-reviewed norm.

4. INTERPRET ASYMMETRY HONESTLY. Peak-force test-retest CV in climbers is ~5.6% (McClean 2023, n=13). Typical real between-hand difference in male climbers is 4.1% (Hartley 2023, n=36). So anything under roughly 10% is indistinguishable from measurement noise plus normal handedness. Do not act on it. Only a persistent difference >15% across two separate test days is worth a conversation, and even then no study links finger asymmetry to climbing performance or injury.

5. CRITICAL FORCE TEST (dominant arm only, once per block). Rest 10 minutes after the max attempts, or better, do this on a separate Monday. Open the app's Critical Force test. Same setup, same arm position. The protocol is 24 repetitions of 7 seconds maximal pull / 3 seconds rest = 4 minutes continuous. Pull as hard as you can EVERY rep including the first. Do not pace yourself — pacing invalidates the test. Your force will fall steeply for the first ~2 minutes and then flatten out. The flat part is the point of the test.

6. READ OFF THREE NUMBERS: CF (mean force of the last 3 contractions, what the app reports), W' (impulse above CF), and CFmin (the LOWEST single contraction of the last three). Also record CF as % of bodyweight.

7. SET YOUR SUB-THRESHOLD CEILING. Baláš et al. 2024 (n=12) showed the app's CF number overestimates what is actually sustainable: only 1 of 12 climbers could hold their calculated CF for 12 minutes, while 92% could complete a trial at CF minus 6 kg. So your working ceiling = CFmin, or CF minus 6 kg, whichever is LOWER. Write that number on the wall next to the hangboard. Every sub-threshold session for the next block is prescribed in kg against that number, not as a guessed % of max.

8. SANITY-CHECK YOUR CURRENT 45% DOSE. In climbers, critical force sits at about 41% of MVC on average (Fryer 2019). After the ~6 kg correction, genuinely sustainable force is nearer 30-35% of one-arm max. If your existing sub-threshold hangs are set at 45%, they are probably ABOVE your true metabolic threshold — i.e. they are accumulating fatigue, not just flushing. This is the single most useful thing this test session buys you.
9. Log everything in one spreadsheet with the date, and the setup notes. Do not test more often than every 4-6 weeks.

'Same setup, forever.' Arm position changes measured finger force materially — Baláš's arm-position work found bent-arm fixation produced roughly 62 N less than straight-arm. Change nothing between tests.
On the CF test: 'every rep is a max rep.' The information is in how far you fall, not how long you last.

Your third max attempt is more than ~10% below your first — you are testing fatigue, not strength. Stop and retest another day.
You have climbed hard within the previous 48 hours. Reschedule; the test is worthless when pre-fatigued.

evidence.transfer: Transfer to CLIMBING performance is ASSUMED, not demonstrated. No study has trained climbers with sub-threshold unilateral load-cell contractions and measured redpoint grade, on-route recovery, or route endurance. The only controlled trial in the neighbourhood (Devise 2022) trained at 60% bilaterally on a hangboard and measured hangboard stamina and endurance — lab proxies, not climbing. The reoxygenation mechanism (Fryer 2015) is cross-sectional: it shows elite climbers reoxygenate faster, not that training at 40% makes you reoxygenate faster.
evidence.summary: Be clear about what is and is not supported. The CLOSEST controlled evidence is Devise, Lechaptois, Berton & Vigouroux (2022, Front Sports Act Living, n=54 climbers in 4 groups): 4 weeks, 2x/week on a 12 mm edge. The F60 group (60% of max, 10 s hang / 6 s rest, x24, bilateral, n=14) improved stamina from 32.6% to 53.5% and endurance from 65.7% to 78.5%, with only a non-significant strength trend (+5.9%, p=0.07) — i.e. low-intensity intermittent finger work moved endurance measures without moving strength, which is exactly the profile wanted here. But that study used 60%, bilateral, twice a week, and measured lab proxies. Gilmore, Klimek, Abrahamsson & Baar (2024, n=526 observational, self-reported app data) found ~40% low-intensity 'Abrahangs' ALONE produced +2.5% strength that was NOT statistically significant (p=0.1216, Cohen's d 0.29 vs climbing-only), while max hangs alone gave +3.2%

blocks.name: The work
steps: 1. Start with the WEAKER arm (from the calibration day) so it never gets the fatigued slot.
2. Set up and pre-load the block until the app shows a couple of kilos, so the first rep does not start with a snatch.
3. On the app's cue, build to the target force over about 1 second, then HOLD it flat for the remaining 6 seconds. The screen should show a plateau, not a spike-and-sag. Release smoothly.

4. During the 3-second rest, fully let go and drop the hand to your side and shake it loose. Do not just relax the fingers on the block. Recovery with the forearm shaken beside the body increased intermittent test time by 22% and reoxygenation rate by 32% versus leaving the hand on the hold (Baláš et al. 2016) — the rest position is part of the dose.
5. Complete 12 reps = 2 minutes. Put the block down. Rest 2 full minutes seated, doing nothing with the forearms.
6. Repeat on the other arm. Then a second set on each arm, same order. Total: 4 sets, 8 minutes of work, ~12 minutes elapsed.

7. HOW TO KNOW IT IS WORKING (within the session): the last rep of the last set should look like the first rep — a flat plateau at target with no visible sag, and you should be able to hold the target with the same effort. If reps 9-12 of any set start sagging below target, the load is too high; drop it 2 kg next time.

8. HOW TO KNOW IT IS WORKING (across the block): at the next calibration day, CF and CF-as-%-of-max should rise while max stays flat. That is the endurance-specific signature you are after. Max going up and CF staying flat means you have accidentally made this a strength session.
9. COMMON ERROR #1: leaning back or driving with the lat so the load cell reads high while the fingers do less. Keep the torso vertical and the shoulder quiet — the arm should be a passive strut.

10. COMMON ERROR #2: creeping the load up week to week because it feels easy. It is SUPPOSED to feel easy. The entire point of the constraint is that this is not a third hard finger day, and creeping it up converts it into one.
11. COMMON ERROR #3: letting the wrist deviate toward the pinky as you fatigue. Reset the wrist between every rep.
12. Frequency: 3-4 times per week maximum, always at least 6 hours away from any other finger loading, and never on Monday or Thursday.

dailyMenu.name: Pre-Session Dynamic Warm-Up
dailyMenu.dose: 3 min pulse-raise + 5 min dynamic shoulder/hip movements + a 3-step progressive finger ramp (30/50/70% of max) — and ZERO static stretching of the forearms or finger flexors before Monday or Thursday.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: This is not an alternative to a training day, it is a prefix to Monday and Thursday. Choose to add it whenever a session has felt sluggish for the first 15 minutes, or whenever the first max hang of the day reads noticeably below the second or third on the Tindeq. It is also the correct answer to 'should I stretch before climbing?' — the answer is yes, dynamically, and specifically not the forearms.

evidence.transfer: PARTIALLY DEMONSTRATED, in a climbing population, but on lab proxies rather than climbing performance. The 2025 crossover trial was run on actual rock climbers and showed real acute changes in shoulder ROM, upper-limb strength and dynamic stability — but it measured no climb, no grade, no send. So 'dynamic warm-up improves climbing' remains unproven; 'dynamic warm-up acutely improves shoulder ROM and upper-limb force in climbers without hurting finger strength' is demonstrated. The negative instruction is on firmer ground: the grip-force decrement from finger-flexor static stretching is a direct measurement of the exact capacity their Monday session depends on, in a controlled crossover, with a plausible neural mechanism and a contralateral effect that rules out pure mechanical explanation. Of everything in this whole domain, the instruction 'stop static stretching your forearms before hangboarding' is the item most likely to actually change an outcome the athlete cares about — and it costs nothing.
evidence.summary: Two controlled trials, both relevant, neither measuring climbing grade. POSITIVE side: the only warm-up study ever run in climbers — a 2025 randomized, counterbalanced crossover in J Sports Sci Med with 22 recreational rock climbers — compared 10 minutes each of dynamic stretching with Thera-Band, vibration rolling, and a climbing-specific warm-up. All three significantly improved shoulder flexion, internal rotation, external rotation, overhead flexibility, and Upper Quarter Y-Balance (all p < 0.05). All three increased elbow flexor and shoulder extensor strength. Critically, NONE of them increased finger flexor strength, so none of them is a substitute for the progressive finger ramp. Vibration rolling beat the other two for shoulder flexion and external rotation ROM; the climbing-specific warm-up beat dynamic stretching for shoulder external rotator strength (p = 0.04).
