setup: Floor space. A broomstick, towel, or the rope from the pulley system for shoulder pass-throughs.
The hangboard, or the Tindeq + Port-A-Board, used only for the progressive ramp, not for work.
A clock or phone timer.
warmup: This IS the warm-up. The 3 minutes of pulse-raise below is its own warm-up.

blocks.name: The work
steps: 1) PULSE RAISE, 3 minutes. Anything that gets you warm and slightly out of breath and does not load the fingers: jumping jacks, skipping on the spot, brisk stairs, or fast bodyweight squats. The target is to feel genuinely warm and to have broken a very light sweat. COMMON ERROR: skipping straight to the movements while cold. Tissue temperature is doing more work here than any of the stretches.

2) SHOULDER PASS-THROUGHS, 10 reps. Hold a broomstick or towel in both hands, arms straight, hands very wide. Keeping the arms locked straight, raise it overhead and take it back behind you as far as you comfortably can, then return. If you cannot get it behind your head, widen your grip. COMMON ERROR: bending the elbows to cheat it behind you. Narrow the grip only when you can do it with locked elbows.
3) ARM CIRCLES, 15 forward and 15 backward, building from small to as large as you can make them.

4) SCAPULAR PUSH-UPS, 10 reps. In a push-up plank with arms locked straight, let your chest sink between your shoulder blades (blades squeeze together), then push the floor away so your upper back rounds. Elbows stay locked the whole time. Only the shoulder blades move.
5) DEEP SQUATS, 10 reps, sinking to the deepest position you can hold with heels down, pausing 1 second at the bottom.
6) LEG SWINGS, 15 per leg forward-back then 15 per leg side-to-side, building the amplitude over the set.
7) SHOULDER EXTERNAL ROTATION, 15 slow reps per side with a light band or a very light plate — this one you already have in the menu; it belongs here as a warm-up dose, not a training dose.

8) PROGRESSIVE FINGER RAMP, 3 pulls per hand. On the Port-A-Board's 20mm edge or an open-hand jug/large rung, pull to roughly 30% of your max for 5 seconds, rest 1 min; then 50% for 5 seconds, rest 1 min; then 70% for 5 seconds, rest 2 min. Then start the session. COMMON ERROR: going straight from cold hands to a max hang. YOU KNOW IT IS WORKING when your first working set of the session is your best, not your third.

9) DO NOT DO: any static stretch of the finger flexors, forearm flexors, or wrist (the classic 'palm out, pull the fingers back' stretch) before a finger session. Save it for after, or for a non-finger day, or skip it entirely.

cues: Warm first, then move. Cold dynamic stretching is just cold stretching.
Dynamic means moving through range repeatedly, not holding a position.
Build amplitude across the set — first swing is small, last swing is your biggest.
Never static-stretch the forearms before hangs. Hold that thought for post-session at the earliest.
If the first max hang is always your worst, the warm-up is too short, not the fingers too weak.
stopIf: Any pain during the ramp pulls at 30% or 50% — that is diagnostic information, not something to warm up through. Stop the session's finger work.
You feel more fatigued after the warm-up than before it. Ten minutes should cost you nothing.
Shoulder pain during pass-throughs — widen the grip until it disappears; if it does not, stop that movement.

dailyMenu.name: Forearm Rotation Eccentrics
dailyMenu.dose: 3x/week on non-finger days: 3x15 slow 4-second eccentric SUPINATION + 3x15 slow 4-second eccentric PRONATION per arm, with a single 5 lb plate gripped by the rim (unbalanced lever) — about 9 minutes total.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Pick this on any Tue/Wed/Fri/Sat slot, and pick it preferentially over the next 8-10 weeks while hang volume is ramping — that ramp is exactly when medial elbow pain shows up in climbers. It is the only item in the whole menu that loads forearm pronation/supination; wrist extension (which the athlete already does) does not train this plane at all. Choose it over the shoulder circuit on any day when the elbows feel 'used' after a board session but the shoulders feel fine.

evidence.transfer: NO demonstrated transfer to climbing performance, and none is claimed — this is not a performance exercise and will not make them climb 5.12a. Transfer to reduced ELBOW INJURY in climbers is weakly demonstrated: it was one component of a bundled intervention in one low-quality RCT in a cohort demographically similar to them. Transfer to reduced injury in an asymptomatic person is entirely assumed — both Tyler trials treated people who already had tendinopathy. The mechanistic story (loading the flexor-pronator and extensor-supinator masses in a plane climbing never trains, in a person whose finger flexors are outpacing everything attached to the same epicondyles) is plausible but unproven. Rated 'controlled-trial' on the strength of the trials that exist, not because those trials are good.
evidence.summary: Three converging but individually weak sources. (1) CLIMBING-SPECIFIC: Kozin et al. randomised 84 male amateur student climbers (40 intervention / 44 control, aged 18-19, 2.2-2.4 years climbing experience) to one year of usual training vs usual training plus a 15-minute battery 3-4x/week (150 sessions). Slow eccentric forearm pronation with a 4 kg dumbbell, 5-10 reps, was one of the three named intervention exercises. Elbow paper (Physiother Q 2022;30(2):90-99) reported significantly reduced incidence rate ratio for moderate and severe elbow injuries; the companion paper from the same cohort (Phys Educ Students 2021) reported odds of mild elbow injury 4.625x higher in control (95% CI 1.198-17.854) and moderate 5.588x higher (95% CI 1.143-27.324). (2) TREATMENT EVIDENCE FOR THE SAME MOVEMENT: Tyler et al., J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2010;19(6):917-22 randomised 21 patients with chronic lateral

setup: ONE small plate — 5 lb to start, 2.5 lb if that feels heavy. Grip it by the RIM so the mass hangs off one side of your fist. You need an unbalanced lever, not a balanced dumbbell; a balanced weight makes the exercise nearly useless.
A claw hammer held by the end of the handle works identically and is easier to grip — use whichever you actually have to hand.
A chair, and a table edge or your own thigh to rest the forearm on.
Nothing else. No FlexBar needed — the plate/hammer version is the exercise that was actually in the climbing trial (Kozin used a 4 kg dumbbell held vertically).
warmup: 30 s: shake the arms out, then open and close both hands 20 times.
20 slow, pain-free wrist circles each direction with no weight.
One set of 10 unloaded pronation/supination through the full arc, so you know where your end range is before you add load.

blocks.name: The work
steps: 1. SET UP THE ARM. Sit. Lay your forearm along your thigh (or a table) so the wrist and hand hang off the end with nothing under them. Elbow bent about 90 degrees and tucked lightly against your ribs. From here the forearm never moves — only the hand rotates. If the elbow drifts away from your side, the weight is too heavy.
2. HOLD THE WEIGHT. Grip the plate by its rim (or the hammer by the end of the handle) so the mass clearly hangs to one side of your fist.

3. ECCENTRIC SUPINATION SET. Start with the loaded hand rotated palm-DOWN. Reach across with your FREE hand, take hold of the loaded hand, and use the free hand to rotate it all the way to palm-UP. The free hand does 100% of that lifting. Now let go with the free hand, and lower the weight back down to palm-down over a slow four-second count, resisting the whole way. That slow lowering IS the exercise. 15 reps = 1 set. Rest 60 s. Do 3 sets.
4. ECCENTRIC PRONATION SET. Same setup. Use the free hand to rotate the loaded hand all the way to palm-DOWN. Let go, and lower slowly back to palm-up over four seconds. 15 reps, 3 sets, 60 s rest.
5. Repeat both blocks on the other arm. Both arms, both directions, every session.
6. FREQUENCY. Three times a week on days that are NOT Monday and NOT Thursday. Never in the 12 hours before a hard finger session.

7. PROGRESSION RULE. Only add load when you have completed 3x15 at a genuine 4-second lower, with zero elbow soreness the next morning, for two consecutive weeks. Then add 2.5 lb. That is a slow ramp on purpose — this is the tissue that goes wrong when climbers ramp fast.

cues: 'The forearm is a fence post. Only the hand turns.' Shoulder shrugging or the elbow flaring out means drop the weight.
Count the lower out loud: 'one-thousand-one … one-thousand-four.' Almost everyone does two seconds and believes they did four.

BIGGEST ERROR: lifting the weight back up with the working arm. The working muscle must never shorten under load. The free hand always does the lift. Eccentric-only is the whole point of the protocol.
SECOND ERROR: shortening the arc. Go from fully palm-up to fully palm-down — the end range is where the tendon actually gets loaded.

HOW YOU KNOW IT'S WORKING: within 3-4 weeks the forearm feels more controlled and less 'jangly' at the end of a board session, and your pain-free grip measured on the Tindeq immediately after a hard session drops less than it used to.
stopIf: Sharp, pinpoint pain on the bony bump on either side of the elbow during the lowering phase — as opposed to a diffuse muscular burn. Halve the weight.
Any medial (inside) elbow soreness still present 48 hours later. Skip the next session and halve the load.
Any numbness or tingling into the ring/little finger — that is ulnar nerve territory. Stop the exercise entirely and get it assessed.
If Monday's max hangs or Thursday's board session feel weaker than usual, you are going too heavy or doing this too close to those days. Move it further from them.
If soreness persists past two consecutive weeks at the lowest load, drop the exercise. This is prehab, not a training goal.
log: Pain-free grip max on the Tindeq (both hands, once weekly, same time of day, same posture) — this is the stand
Load (lb) x reps x tempo per session, per arm.
Morning elbow soreness 0-10, logged separately for medial (inside) and lateral (outside).
Count of days per month with any elbow discomfort — the number that actually matters for an October goal.

how.gist: Your FREE hand turns the weight palm-up. The working hand lowers it back, slowly.
steps: Sit. Forearm flat along your thigh, hand hanging off past the knee.
Elbow bent ~90° and tucked against your ribs. The forearm never moves — only the hand turns.
Hold a 5 lb plate by its RIM so the weight clearly hangs off one side of your fist.
Start palm-DOWN. Reach across with your free hand and turn the loaded hand palm-UP.
Let go with the free hand and lower back to palm-down over a slow 4-second count. 15 reps.
how.watch: Never lift the weight with the working arm. The free hand does 100% of every lift — the slow lowering is the whole exercise.
how.easier: A claw hammer held at the end of the handle works identically and is easier to grip.

how.gist: Same thing the other way: free hand turns it palm-DOWN, you lower to palm-up.
steps: Same seat, same forearm on the thigh, same plate held by the rim.
Start palm-UP. Use the free hand to turn the loaded hand palm-DOWN.
Let go, and lower back to palm-up over a slow 4-second count.
15 reps, 60 seconds rest, 3 sets. Then do both directions on the other arm.
how.watch: Count it out loud — 'one-thousand-one … one-thousand-four'. Almost everyone does two seconds and believes they did four.

dailyMenu.name: Weekly Load Audit + 4-Question Body Check
dailyMenu.dose: Every Sunday evening, 4 minutes: score the 4 OSTRC questions (0/8/17/25 each) separately for fingers, elbow and shoulder, log the week's high-strain finger exposure count and total hang volume, then apply one non-negotiable rule — any area scoring above 0 for two consecutive weeks means next Monday's hang volume drops by one third.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: This is not an alternative to a training session — it is a fixed 4-minute Sunday appointment that runs alongside everything else. Its whole reason for existing is their Sjöman subgroup risk: for a male climber with under 6 years in the sport performing at 7a+, the evidence points at fingerboard LOAD as the hazard, not at a missing exercise. Nothing you can add to the menu addresses that; only a rule that catches load creep does. Prioritise setting this up in the first week after the Tindeq arrives, because that is when hang volume is most likely to drift upward without anyone noticing.

evidence.transfer: Zero transfer to climbing PERFORMANCE — it is not a training stimulus and will not add a single grade. Transfer to reduced injury is ASSUMED, not demonstrated: no trial anywhere has shown that self-monitoring prevents injury. What IS demonstrated is that the questionnaire validly detects overuse problems earlier than time-loss definitions do (n=313, 5 sports), and that their exact demographic slice shows a positive association between regular fingerboarding and finger pain in cross-sectional data (n=75, P=0.03). The honest framing is: this is the cheapest available way to notice the thing the evidence says is most likely to derail them, and it costs 4 minutes a week — not that it has been proven to work.
evidence.summary: Split this into two claims, because they have very different evidence. CLAIM 1 — the instrument measures something real: the OSTRC Overuse Injury Questionnaire was developed and validated by Clarsen et al. (Br J Sports Med 2013) in a 13-week prospective study of 313 athletes across five sports (cross-country skiing, floorball, handball, road cycling, volleyball), and is now used in national Olympic and Paralympic monitoring programmes. It reliably captures low-grade overuse problems that conventional time-loss injury definitions miss entirely. That claim is well supported. CLAIM 2 — that monitoring and acting on the score REDUCES injury: this has never been tested in a trial, in climbing or in any other sport. There is no RCT of injury surveillance as an intervention. So the instrument is validated; the intervention is expert consensus. WHY IT IS THE RIGHT TARGET FOR HIM: Sjöman, Grønhau

setup: A notes app or a spreadsheet with one row per week.
Your Tindeq log.
Nothing else. This costs nothing and takes 4 minutes.
warmup: None required — this is a desk task, not a training session.

blocks.name: The work
steps: 1. Same time every week (Sunday evening — pick a time and never move it). For EACH of three areas separately (FINGERS, ELBOW, SHOULDER), answer four questions. For every question the only allowed answers are 0, 8, 17 or 25: Q1 'Have you had difficulty participating in climbing because of problems in this area this week?' (0 = no difficulty, 8 = to a minor extent, 17 = to a moderate extent, 25 = cannot participate at all). Q2 'To what extent have you reduced your climbing volume because of it?' (same scale). Q3 'To what extent has it affected your performance?' (same scale). Q4 'To what extent have you experienced pain in this area?' (same scale). Add the four = a 0-100 score for that area. Anything above 0 counts as a problem; 0 is the target.

2. Log the objective load numbers for the week, honestly: number of HIGH-STRAIN FINGER EXPOSURES (target: exactly 2 — Monday and Thursday); total number of max hangs plus repeater reps on Monday; total board attempts on Thursday; and any accidental third exposure — an unplanned session, a hard boulder outdoors, a day of moving furniture, a long belay session on steep terrain. Accidental third exposures are the single most common way a 2-day rule quietly becomes a 3-day rule.

3. APPLY THE RULE WITHOUT NEGOTIATION. Any area scoring above 0 in TWO CONSECUTIVE weeks → the following Monday's hang volume drops by one third, and the smallest edge used goes up one size (20 mm becomes 25 mm). Re-score the week after.

4. ESCALATION. Any area scoring 17 or 25 on Q1 or Q4 in a SINGLE week → skip the next high-strain finger session entirely and substitute the sub-threshold ~45% hangs already in the menu. One skipped session in August costs nothing against an October goal; six weeks off in September costs the goal.

5. MONTHLY. Record Tindeq max on the 20 mm and pain-free grip. A falling max alongside a rising finger score is the textbook overload picture and should trigger a deload immediately, not a 'push through it'.

6. Chart three lines over the season: weekly OSTRC finger score, weekly high-strain exposures, and monthly Tindeq max. The pattern you are looking for is flat-at-zero score, flat-at-two exposures, slowly rising max.

cues: Answer fast and honestly. The score is only useful if you don't argue with it after the fact.
The point is not the number, it is the TREND. One bad week is noise; two consecutive weeks is a signal.

BIGGEST ERROR: treating a score of 8 as 'basically nothing'. An 8 is precisely the early low-grade complaint this instrument was built to catch — the kind that never stops you climbing until suddenly it does.
SECOND ERROR: under-counting exposures. A hard outdoor boulder session is a finger exposure. A long session of steep pumpy autobelay laps is a finger exposure. Count them.
HOW YOU KNOW IT'S WORKING: exposures sit at exactly 2/week and the finger score sits at 0 through an entire training block while the Tindeq max still climbs.
stopIf: If the finger score climbs three weeks running despite deloading, stop hangboarding entirely until it returns to 0, and book a hand therapist. Do not negotiate this against the October date.
If you find yourself editing past entries to make the trend look better, the tool has stopped working — get someone else to hold you to the rule.
log: Weekly OSTRC-style score, 0-100, separately for fingers, elbow and shoulder — the primary chart.
High-strain finger exposures per week (target line at 2, hard ceiling at 3).
Weekly hang volume: total max hangs + repeater reps.
Monthly Tindeq 20 mm max and pain-free grip.

dailyMenu.name: Climbing-Shaped Core
dailyMenu.dose: 2x/week (Tue + Sat), 48h+ from finger days: 3x8 hanging foot-lifts on the jug rail, then 3 rounds of dynamic plank-reach 8 + dynamic side bridge 6/side — 14 min, total hang time under 3 min on a jug at roughly 25–35% of finger capacity.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Pick this over the day's default on Tuesday or Saturday (both are 48h+ from Monday's hangs and Thursday's board), especially in the 2–3 weeks after a gym session where their feet cut unintentionally on the steeper Tension Board angles or where their hips sagged away from the wall. Also pick it when the athlete wants a session that feels like real training but spends zero finger budget. Do NOT pick it on Monday or Thursday, and do not pick it the day before Thursday.

evidence.transfer: NOT DEMONSTRATED. No study has ever shown that core training raises a climber's grade. The single climber trial measured lab and climbing-shaped tests only, had no non-training control group, and its authors explicitly flag that core training was not performed in isolation. Cross-sectionally the link is weak: leg-raise correlates with grade at r=0.30–0.45, momentum absorption at r=−0.01 to 0.31, fishing kicks at r=−0.42 to −0.12; the plank distinguishes lower-grade from intermediate climbers but not intermediate from advanced; Draper et al. found no leg-raise differences between ability levels at all. Mermier 2000 attributed 58.9% of performance variance to a trainable strength/endurance component with no core factor identified. The mechanistic case (better trunk stiffness lets you transfer weight to your feet on steep terrain and pull less hard with your hands, therefore lower forearm occlusion) is plausible and untested. Buy this as cheap, finger-free insurance that plausibly helps on the steeper Tension Board angles; do not let it displace a single minute of the endurance work.
evidence.summary: One randomised trial exists in climbers: Saeterbakken, Loken, Scott, Hermans, Vereide & Andersen, PLOS ONE 2018;13(10):e0203766 — 19 advanced-to-elite climbers randomised (18 completers, 9 per group; 14 male, 4 female; mean age 27.4±6.7; red-point IRCRA 19), 10 weeks, 2 sessions/week, 30–40 min, four exercises (foot-lift on a pending wall, arm lock-off, side-bridge, prone-bridge), 3–4 sets of 4–10RM, progressed by wall steepness, base of support and target distance. Results: body-lift +29.6% (p=0.037) isometric and +33.8% (p=0.100) dynamic; trunk flexion MVC +10.8% (p=0.029) and +8.7% (p=0.045); trunk rotation improved significantly only in the dynamic group (right +8.2%, p=0.012; left +14.9%, p=0.043); superman +5.0% (p=0.041) dynamic only; body lock-off did NOT improve significantly in either group (+10.6% vs −0.5%); finger hang unchanged (+4.1%/+4.5%, NS). No between-group differences

setup: Mount or locate the large rounded top rail / jug of the Frictitious board, or the pull-up jugs, free-hanging on the joists. Do not use the 20/15mm rungs, the pockets, the rock crimps, or the Crux block for any of this — none of this session touches an edge.

Optional finger-free variant: drape a folded towel or a sling over the rail and hold the towel instead of the wood. This removes essentially all edge loading and is the preferred version on any week where the fingers feel at all tender.

Foot target: girth-hitch a sling, a length of webbing, or a knotted towel around a joist about 1 m to the side of the hangboard, hanging so the bottom of the loop sits roughly level with their hips when the athlete is hanging with straight arms. If ceiling height puts their feet close to the floor, just start each rep with knees slightly bent and keep them bent — the drill still works.
Floor: a yoga mat, folded blanket or towel for the bridges. That is the entire equipment list.
Have a timer or phone stopwatch visible.
warmup: 10 slow cat-cow on hands and knees — arch and round the spine over about 3 seconds each way.

10 dead bugs: lie on your back, arms straight up at the ceiling, hips and knees at 90 degrees. Press your low back flat into the floor and keep it flat while you slowly lower one arm overhead and the opposite leg toward the floor over 3 seconds, then return. If your low back lifts off the floor, you went too far — shorten the range.

One 30-second ACTIVE hang on the jug rail: hang with straight arms but pull your shoulder blades down and slightly back so your ears are not buried between your shoulders. This is a rehearsal of the position, not a strength effort.

blocks.name: The work
steps: STEP 1 — Hanging foot-lift, 3 sets of 8 total reps (4 per side), 60–75 seconds rest between sets. Hang from the jug rail with a shoulder-width overhand grip. Arms straight. Before every set, set the shoulders: pull the shoulder blades down and toward each other so you feel your lats switch on and your neck lengthen — you should NOT feel like you are dangling in the joint. Then set the trunk: pull the bottom of your ribcage down toward your pelvis and tuck your tailbone slightly forward so your low back flattens. Now, without any swinging, lift one knee toward your chest and place or lightly touch the ball of that foot into the hanging sling loop. Hold there for one second, then lower over 2 seconds until the leg is straight (or back to the bent start). That is one rep. Alternate sides each rep.

STEP 1 COMMON ERRORS: (a) Generating the lift with a body swing or a small pull-up from the arms — if the joists creak, if your body pendulums, or if your chest rises toward the rail, you cheated; slow down and cut the range. (b) Leaving the pelvis in an arched position (butt out, low back hollow) — that turns the whole thing into a pure hip-flexor lift and you will feel it in the front of the hip crease instead of the abdomen. (c) Holding your breath for the whole set — breathe out through pursed lips as the knee comes up.

STEP 1 REGRESSION AND PROGRESSION: If you cannot reach the sling without swinging, ignore the sling and just do hanging knee raises to 90 degrees. Once 3x8 to the sling is smooth, progress in this order: raise the sling 10 cm, then again, then switch from knee-lift to a straight-leg foot-lift, then to touching the loop with the outside edge of the foot or the heel (heel-hook shape). Do not add weight — change the lever and the height instead.

STEP 2 — Dynamic prone bridge with reach, 3 sets of 8 total reaches (4 per side). Set up face down on forearms: elbows directly under shoulders, forearms flat, feet about hip-width, body in one straight line from ear to ankle. Squeeze your glutes hard and tuck your pelvis so the low back flattens — this is the position, and it should already feel like work. From there, slowly slide and reach ONE arm forward along the floor until it is fully extended overhead, taking 2 seconds out and 2 seconds back, while the hips stay absolutely square to the floor. Alternate arms.

STEP 2 COMMON ERRORS: hips sagging toward the floor, hips piking up into an upside-down V, or — the big one — the hips rotating as the arm goes out. Have them film one set from the side and one from behind. If the hip on the reaching side rises, widen the feet slightly and reach less far. How to know it is working: the burn should be a deep brace across the front of the abdomen and down the side you are NOT reaching with. If it is a low-back ache, the brace failed — regress to a plain 20-second plank hold with a hard glute squeeze until that is easy.

STEP 3 — Dynamic side bridge, 3 sets of 6 per side. Lie on your side, elbow directly under the shoulder, forearm flat and pointing straight ahead, feet stacked one on top of the other, knees straight. Lift the hips so shoulder, hip and ankle form one straight line. From that position, lower the hip about 5 cm toward the floor over 2 seconds, then press back up to the line over 1 second. That is one rep.

STEP 3 COMMON ERRORS: the top shoulder rolling forward (chest should stay pointing at the wall, not at the floor), and the hips drifting behind the line so you are half-sitting. Progression once 3x6 per side is easy: lift the top leg a few inches and hold it there (star side plank), then move to a straight-arm side plank with the hand under the shoulder.

STRUCTURE: do Step 1 as three straight sets first. Then alternate Step 2 and Step 3 as a superset for three rounds with about 45 seconds rest between rounds. Total working time lands around 14 minutes including the warm-up.

PROGRESSION OVER THE BLOCK: run it for 8–10 weeks, which matches the trial's 10 weeks and the ~8.6-week mean of the trunk-training meta-analysis. Add difficulty by raising the foot target, lengthening the lever, and slowing the tempo — never by adding sets past 4 or by adding a third weekly session.

dailyMenu.name: Hip Abduction Block
dailyMenu.dose: 2x6/side loaded Cossack squats + 2x8 90/90 rotations + 3x30s loaded straddle sit + 2x30s/side standing straddle, 3-4x/week, holding each stretch at ~7/10 intensity, never into sharp pain.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Pick this on Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday or Sunday — any day that is NOT Monday or Thursday, and ideally not within 3 hours before them. It is a zero-finger-load day filler. evidence.transfer: TRANSFER TO CLIMBING IS ASSUMED, NOT DEMONSTRATED. There is no trial — randomized or otherwise — showing that a hip mobility program improves climbing grade, climbing economy, or any climbing outcome. What is demonstrated is (a) this kind of work reliably increases hip range of motion in RCTs of non-climbers, and (b) in one cross-sectional sample of 29 male 7b-8c climbers, better hip abduction was moderately associated with higher grade. The causal arrow in (b) is unknown: climbing steep rock for years may simply produce hip abduction range rather than the reverse. And the ceiling is probably low — Mermier 2000 found the entire flexibility component uniquely explained 1.8% of climbing performance variance (n=44). Expect this to change how certain moves feel, not to move their grade. It earns its place only because it costs zero finger exposure.
evidence.summary: Split cleanly into two claims. CLAIM 1, that this raises hip range of motion: strongly supported by meta-analyses of RCTs, but only for the ROM outcome. Afonso 2021 (Healthcare; 11 RCTs, 452 participants) found strength training and stretching produce statistically indistinguishable ROM gains (ES -0.22, 95% CI -0.55 to 0.12, p = 0.206, I-squared 65.4%), which is why the loaded Cossack squat is in here rather than more passive holding. setup: Clear ~7 ft of floor width plus a clear stretch of bare wall.
One plate, roughly 10-25 lb, held at the chest as a counterweight for the Cossack squat. Heavier is not better here; it is for balance, not load.
A tape measure and a piece of tape on the wall at hip height for the monthly measurements.
Optional: a 1 cm book or thin plate to put under a heel, and a 4-6 inch stack of plates/books to sit on.
warmup: 2 min: 20 forward-and-back leg swings per leg holding a wall, then 20 side-to-side leg swings per leg. Swing to a comfortable range, not maximum.
10 bodyweight squats going as deep as you comfortably can, pausing 1 second at the bottom of each.
10 standing hip circles per leg: knee up to hip height, then sweep the knee out to the side and back down.

blocks.name: The work
steps: 1) COSSACK SQUAT — 2 sets of 6 per side. Stand with feet about double shoulder width, toes turned out maybe 20 degrees, holding the plate at your chest with both hands. Shift your weight over the right leg and sit straight down over it as far as you can, keeping the right heel FLAT on the floor. The left leg stays completely straight, left heel on the floor, left toes pulled up toward the ceiling. Pause 2 seconds at the bottom, then push back to the middle and immediately go down over the left. That is one rep per side. COMMON ERROR: the heel of the squatting leg lifts and the straight leg's knee quietly bends — both of those delete the stretch. Fix it by putting a 1 cm book under the squatting heel and going less deep. YOU KNOW IT IS WORKING when you feel a strong pull along the inner thigh of the STRAIGHT leg, not a pinch at the front of the hip of the bent leg.

2) 90/90 HIP ROTATIONS — 2 sets of 8 rotations. Sit on the floor. Right leg in front of you, bent 90 degrees at both hip and knee, so the right shin runs across your body. Left leg out to the side, thigh pointing away from you, also bent 90 degrees, so the left shin runs behind you. Sit up tall, chest up, hands lightly on the floor behind you for support. Now, without using your hands to push, lift both knees, sweep them through the middle, and put them down in the mirror-image position — left leg in front, right leg behind. Take about 3 seconds per rotation. COMMON ERROR: rounding the low back and collapsing backwards, which turns it into a lower-back stretch instead of a hip rotation drill. If you cannot sit upright with both knees down, sit on a 4-6 inch stack of plates or books until you can. YOU KNOW IT IS WORKING when you feel the outer hip/glute of the FRONT leg and a distinct different sensation deep in the front of the BACK leg's hip. STOP if you feel a pinch on the inner side of the rear knee — open that knee angle to 110 degrees instead of 90.

3) LOADED STRADDLE SIT — 3 x 30 seconds. Sit on the floor facing the bare wall, legs opened into as wide a V as you can manage, feet flat against the wall, knees locked straight, toes pointing at the ceiling. Put your hands on the floor in front of you and walk them forward, sliding your hips toward the wall, until the stretch is a strong 7 out of 10 — clearly uncomfortable, definitely not sharp. Hold 30 seconds breathing normally through the nose. Between reps: press both heels hard into the wall for 5 seconds (an isometric contraction, nothing moves), relax completely for 3 seconds, then slide 1-2 cm deeper. COMMON ERROR: bending the knees to get the feet wider, which fakes the range. Keep the knees locked and accept a narrower V.

4) STANDING STRADDLE — 2 x 30 seconds. Feet as wide apart as you can with both feet flat and toes pointing forward (not turned out). Hands on the floor or on a chair. Push your hips backwards and let them sink toward the floor. Hold 30 seconds. This is the training version of the straddle stand test you will measure.

5) ACTIVE STRADDLE LIFTS — 5 per side. Back in the seated straddle (feet off the wall now). Keeping the knee locked, lift one whole leg 2-5 cm off the floor and hold 3 seconds, then lower. This is the step most people skip and it is the one that converts passive range into range you can actually use on a wall. YOU KNOW IT IS WORKING when the lift is hard and shaky — that means you are near the true end of your ACTIVE range, which is the only range that helps you when a foot is out at full stretch.

cues: Strong, never sharp. Aim for 7/10 discomfort. Pain that has an edge to it means back off 10 percent.
Breathe out slowly as you settle into each position; hold your breath and you will fight the stretch.
Both feet flat, both knees locked — the moment a heel lifts or a knee bends you are cheating the range and training nothing.
The last 20 percent of the range is the only part that produces adaptation. Getting to a comfortable position and sitting there does nothing.
On the 90/90, sit TALL first, then rotate. Height of the chest before depth of the hip.
stopIf: Sharp or stabbing groin pain, especially near the pubic bone — stop the session, this is not a stretch you push through.
A pinching sensation at the very front of the hip crease (possible femoroacetabular impingement) — reduce depth by 10 degrees and keep the pinch out of the movement entirely.

Any pain at the sitting bone / high hamstring during the straddle sit. Aggressive straddle work is a known route into high hamstring tendinopathy. Reduce hold intensity to 5/10 and stop leaning forward.
Knee pain in the 90/90, especially on the inside of the rear knee.
Numbness or tingling down either leg.
Any of this leaves you sore enough that Monday's max hangs feel compromised — then it is too much volume, cut to 2x/week.

dailyMenu.tier: HARD · weeks 7–10, replaces Thursday's board block
dailyMenu.name: Bouldering 4×4s
dailyMenu.dose: Four problems three grades below your limit, climbed four times through — sixteen ascents in four circuits, with four to five minutes between circuits rather than the textbook two. This is NOT a third hard day: it replaces the board block of Thursday's gym session. Add Doubled lead laps alongside it as an extra, at two doubles rather than three.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Only on Thursday, only in weeks 7–10, and only by deleting the board block — it is a replacement for that block, never an addition to it. Add Doubled lead laps as an EXTRA on the same day, cut to two doubles: the laps are the most trip-specific work in your week and dropping them entirely turns a route-endurance Thursday into a bouldering session. Choose the 4×4 when Monday went cleanly, your fingers scored 1 or 2 afterwards, your skin is 1 or 2, and you are genuinely walking in the door by 5:45; a 4×4 started at 7pm is a 4×4 you will rush, and rushing is where the pulley goes. Do NOT pick it on a Saturday just because there is budget for a third hard day — the 4×4 is Thursday's replacement for the board block, and a Saturday that goes hard is for the week you miss the gym entirely. Do NOT pick it before week 7: power endurance fades inside a couple of weeks, so a 4×4 block in August is a block you will have fully lost by October, at the cost of the strength base you are building now. Do NOT run it on a day you are also running the repeated-ascent test — that test is the most reliable number you own and a 4×4 in the same session destroys the comparison. In week 10 run it at half volume: two circuits, same intensity, same rest.

evidence.transfer: Transfer to CLIMBING performance is ASSUMED, not demonstrated, and the specific numbers are worse-supported than almost anything else in this plan. No controlled trial has ever trained climbers with a 4×4 and measured a climbing outcome. The famous parameters — four problems, four laps, four minutes, two-to-three grades below limit — have no experimental derivation anywhere in the literature; they are round numbers that propagated through coaching books. Worse, two 2024 RCTs each moved a climbing-specific lab measure with NO corresponding change in bouldering performance (Saeterbakken n=31: finger strength +11.5% vs +5.3%, p=0.021, but bouldering unchanged at p=0.39; Langer n=26: five weeks of on-the-wall board intervals produced no significant between-group difference at all). So the honest position is: the 4×4 is a plausible, physiologically defensible, universally used protocol whose specific prescription is folklore, and whose transfer to a sustained outdoor 5.12a is an inference rather than a finding. It entered this menu because the thing it replaced — Thursday's block A — was labelled power endurance and, at 2–3 minutes of rest between single problems, was not power endurance by any definition. That is no longer the argument for it: block A was rebuilt as board intervals on 2026-08-13, so from week 7 this is a PROGRESSION of a stimulus Thursday already carries — sixteen ascents at higher density instead of twelve — rather than a repair of a session that had none. The two are the same job and are declared `mutex`, so they never land on one day.
evidence.summary: The closest thing to direct evidence is Medernach, Kleinöder & Lötzerich (2015, Sports Technology 8:76–82, n=24 highly-advanced male boulderers randomised to 4 weeks of interval bouldering vs conventional bouldering, 3 × 150 min/wk): climbing time to exhaustion improved +36.2 ± 14.1 s (p<0.001) in the interval group vs +6.1 ± 19.3 s (p=0.298) in controls, with intermittent finger-hang time improving only in the interval group. That is interval bouldering, not a 4×4; elite boulderers, not intermediate route climbers; time to exhaustion, not redpoint grade. Stien et al. (2023, Biology of Sport) meta-analysed 11 studies / 225 climbers and concluded interval-style bouldering 'may' improve climbing — but could not meta-analyse climbing-performance outcomes at all, median PEDro 6/10, no study blinded assessors. The rest-length prescription here comes from Fryer et al. (2015, JSCR, n=44): forearm reoxygenation half-time on intermittent contractions at 40% MVC was 8 s in elite climbers and 83 s in intermediates. At 4 minutes an intermediate forearm is ~86% recovered; at 5 minutes, ~92%. That extrapolation is mechanistic, not tested — nobody has measured reoxygenation between 4×4 laps.

protocol.duration: 60–70 min, Thursday, in place of the board block
setup: Tension Board at 25–30°. NOT 40–55° — the middle angle gives sustained flexor loading without limit-crimp spikes, and the spikes are what tear pulleys when you are fatigued.
Pick FOUR problems, three full grades below your limit, 8–12 hand moves each, roughly 25–35 seconds of climbing apiece. The operational test is 'a grade you can flash, but that is hard to flash.'
Order them hardest and steepest first, descending: V4, V4, V3, V3. You want the difficulty front-loaded while you are fresh.
Write the four problems down before you start. Choosing them while pumped is how the session quietly gets easier.
A phone timer with an audible beep, running for the whole session. Untimed chalking and beta talk is the single most common way this workout stops being this workout.
warmup: This is the non-negotiable part. A 4×4 goes from cold to near-maximal sustained flexor load inside two minutes, and a five-minute warm-up before one has been called 'not just irresponsible, dangerous.'
10 min easy movement — traverse, easy boulders, get genuinely warm before you touch the board.
The Pre-Session Dynamic Warm-Up from the add-ons, in full.
4–5 board problems climbing up in difficulty, finishing one grade below your circuit grade.
5 min rest before circuit 1. Total warm-up 30–40 minutes. If you do not have time for the warm-up, you do not have time for the session — run Thursday as written instead.

blocks.name: A · The circuits
steps: 1. One circuit = all four problems, once each, in order.
2. Rest between problems WITHIN a circuit: 30 s in weeks 7–8, 15 s in weeks 9–10. Start on the beep whether or not you feel ready.
3. Rest between circuits: 5:00 in week 7, 4:30 in week 8, 4:00 in weeks 9–10. Do not go below 4:00, and ignore anyone who tells you to.
4. Four circuits. Sixteen ascents. Then stop. Do not run a fifth because you feel good.

5. WHY THE LONG RESTS: an intermediate climber's forearm reoxygenation half-time is roughly 83 seconds where an elite climber's is 8 (Fryer 2015). The textbook 4×4 rest was written for a forearm most intermediates d not have. At 30 s of rest an elite recovers ~93% of their oxygen deficit and you recover about 22%. Circuits 3 and 4 on a short rest are not power endurance, they are low-quality flailing at maximum injury exposure.

6. TARGET: one fall or fewer across all sixteen ascents. Zero falls means it is too easy — add a grade next week, not less rest. Three or more falls means the problems are too hard. Two falls inside a single circuit means abort the circuit.
7. Total climbing time in circuit 4 should be within 10–15% of circuit 1. If circuit 4 takes 40% longer, the dose was wrong, and you write that down rather than repeating it.

blocks.name: B · Finish, and what this session gives up
steps: One easy lap to cool down. No limit bouldering because you feel good.

ADD THE LAPS: this session is only half of a 4×4 Thursday. Add Doubled lead laps as an extra and run TWO doubles rather than three. They are on their own card so they get their own log — they are not optional.

SAY THE TRADE OUT LOUD so it stays deliberate: you are giving up the low-density board volume that feeds the week-9 repeated-ascent retest, and one doubled lead lap. You are buying an actual power-endurance stimulus, which the week did not previously contain.

cues: 'Density, not difficulty.' The stimulus is sixteen ascents close together. Making the problems harder is a different workout.
'Fail from pump, not from power.' If you cannot generate force on move three of a fresh problem, you are accidentally doing a strength session.
'The timer decides, not you.' Rest creep — chalking, brushing, talking beta — is the most common and least noticed way this workout stops working.
'Sixteen, not sixty-four.' Four circuits of four problems is sixteen ascents. Four laps of each problem in each circuit is a different energy system and a well-known way to hurt yourself.
stopIf: Any sharp or localised finger pain, especially at the base of a finger — stop mid-circuit, do not finish it.
Any audible pop or click at a finger base. Session over. That is a pulley.
You are falling off from fatigue rather than difficulty. Sixteen sloppy ascents on board wood is a skin injury with a finger injury attached.
Two falls inside a single circuit — the grade is wrong, stop rather than pushing through.
Medial elbow ache developing mid-session. High-volume flexor work drives it.
A flapper or a hot spot. Skin binds before muscle does on wood, and climbing the last circuits on compromised skin means climbing them with unreliable grip.
It is week 6 or the day of the repeated-ascent retest.

dailyMenu.name: Doubled lead laps
dailyMenu.dose: Climb a comfortable 5.10, lower, and immediately climb it again without resting on the ground. That is one double — about 90 ft of continuous climbing on a 45 ft wall, which is longer than the median outdoor 5.12a. Three doubles, 5 minutes between. Two on any week you also run 4×4s.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: This is the most trip-specific thing in your entire week, and it is the block most likely to get quietly dropped because it is not the exciting part of a gym session. Run it on Thursday as its own session alongside the board, or alongside a 4×4 on the weeks you run one — three doubles normally, two on a 4×4 week, because the 4×4 has already spent the session's fatigue budget. It is also the right answer on a bonus gym day when your fingers are too beaten up for the board: doubled laps at 5.10 load the forearms in the exact pattern the trip asks for without a single hard crimp. Do NOT treat it as optional on 4×4 weeks — cutting the laps to zero converts a route-endurance session into a bouldering session, and the routes are what you are training for. Skip it only if your fingers are genuinely sore, in which case do a single easy lap and go home.

evidence.transfer: Transfer here is more plausible than for anything else in this menu, and it is still not experimental. Nobody has run a trial where climbers did doubled laps and redpoint grade was measured against a control. What can be said precisely: the plan's own target is climbing 5.10+/5.11− efficiently for about 50 feet, arriving at one named rest and actually recovering there. A doubled lap IS that, rehearsed, at a length that exceeds the routes you are going to try. Every other session in this menu is a proxy for it. The one element with a real mechanism behind it is the forced shakeout, and that mechanism is measured — see the summary. Treat this as deliberate practice at the goal task rather than as a physiological stimulus in the way max hangs are.
evidence.summary: The duration and intensity domain is right: Watts (2004, Eur J Appl Physiol) characterised a hard route ascent as a 2–7 minute effort at roughly 20–25 ml/kg/min with lactate elevated for more than 20 minutes afterwards, and Maciejczyk et al. (2022, Front Physiol, n=13) measured intermittent climbing of comparable duration as 59.9% aerobic / 12.9% anaerobic-lactic / 27.2% alactic — the same energetic territory the 4×4 block targets, at a fraction of the injury exposure. The forced shakeout is the best-evidenced single instruction in this session: Balás et al. (2016) found that recovering with the forearm shaken beside the body increased intermittent test time by 22% and reoxygenation rate by 32% versus leaving the hand on the hold.

setup: A 5.10 you can climb comfortably and have climbed before — you want the movement known, so the session is about pacing and recovery rather than reading.

Lead if you have a partner, autobelay if you do not. The autobelay lane is vertical, which makes it easier than lead terrain; if you are on the autobelay, pick something at the top of your comfortable range.
A timer. The 5 minutes between doubles is part of the dose, not a suggestion.
warmup: Two easy laps, well below the working grade, with a couple of minutes between.
If this is following a 4×4 you are already warm — go straight in.

blocks.name: The doubles
steps: 1. Climb the route at a deliberate, even pace. Do not race it.
2. Lower, and IMMEDIATELY set off again without resting on the ground. Clipping straight back in is the whole point — the second lap starts on a forearm that has not recovered.
3. That is one double: roughly 90 ft of continuous climbing on a 45 ft wall, longer than the median outdoor 5.12a.
4. Rest 5 minutes. Sit down. Do not belay a hard burn in your rest.

5. Three doubles on a normal Thursday. TWO on any week you have also run 4×4s — the 4×4 has already spent the session's fatigue budget, and a third double on those weeks buys tiredness rather than fitness.

6. THE PART THAT MATTERS: on the second lap of each double, force a full shakeout at every rest stance even if you do not feel you need it. Shake the arm loose beside your body, do not just relax the fingers on the hold. That specific rest position increased intermittent test time by 22% and reoxygenation rate by 32% in Balás 2016 — the shakeout is a trained skill, and the trip is going to ask for it at exactly one stance on every route.
7. HOW TO KNOW IT IS WORKING (in session): the second lap of double 3 should feel like the second lap of double 1. If it collapses, the route is too hard — drop a grade rather than gutting it out.

8. HOW TO KNOW IT IS WORKING (across the block): the same route at the same grade stops producing a real pump, and the shakeouts start restoring grip instead of just costing you time. That second one is the adaptation you actually want; if you are merely more tolerant of climbing while pumped, you have trained pain tolerance rather than recovery.
9. One easy lap to cool down.

cues: 'Straight back on.' Resting on the ground between the two laps makes it two laps, not a double.
'Shake at every rest, even when you don't need to.' The one instruction here with measured evidence behind it.
'Even pace, not fast.' You are rehearsing efficiency, not racing a clock.
'Two doubles on a 4×4 week.' Three is the normal dose, not the minimum.
stopIf: Any finger pain — this is a low-crimp session, so a finger complaint here means you arrived already damaged.
Your footwork stops being deliberate. Sloppy feet under pump is how ankles get hurt on lead falls.

dailyMenu.name: Wall traverses
dailyMenu.dose: Climb sideways around the gym's walls, low to the ground, taking the biggest holds each panel offers and moving the whole time. Three bouts of about five minutes, four minutes sitting between. Easy is the dose — where the wall turns hard, step off and walk past that section rather than fighting it.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: As the easy tail of a gym night — after 4×4s or the board, when the hard work is spent and you want more time on the wall at a cost of nearly nothing — or as its own low day at the gym when the fingers won't take anything harder. It is deliberately easier than crimp crawls: real footholds carry most of your weight, and the hard panels are there to be skipped, not survived. It is still not a rest day — twenty minutes of continuous climbing is work, just cheap work.

setup: The gym's walls at ground level. The bouldering walls work best — stay low, under the down-climb line, so coming off is a step rather than a fall.
Nothing but shoes and chalk, and a clock you can glance at.
Pick your line before you get on: which panels you will traverse, and which you will step off and walk past. Roofs, blank sections and anything steep are walk-pasts, not challenges.
If this follows a 4×4 or the board you are already warm — go straight in.
warmup: Fresh session only: three or four easy jug problems, then one minute of traversing on the easiest section you have, then start bout 1.

blocks.name: The traverse — around the walls, never still, never fighting
steps: Get on at your start point, feet on real footholds, and move sideways at an even, unhurried pace. Big holds, quiet feet, long arms.
Take the biggest holds each panel offers. This session is easy ON PURPOSE — the intensity dial is hold size and which sections you climb, and the setting is low.
Where the wall turns hard — a steep panel, a bare stretch, someone's project — step off, walk past, get back on. Fighting a hard section turns an endurance session into bouldering.
If the pump builds past a murmur, park on a jug and shake one arm at a time until it fades, then carry on. Getting properly pumped means you are traversing too hard.
A bout is about five minutes of moving — come off wherever you are, sit down for four minutes, go again. Three bouts, two if this is riding on the back of a 4×4.

cues: Slow is the skill. You are buying time on the wall, not distance around it.
Feet first — look at the foothold, place it silently, then move a hand.
Hang on the skeleton. Long arms between moves instead of pulling through bent elbows.
If a section makes you grit your teeth, that section is not part of this workout.

Form collapses: feet start skating, or you are hauling through bent arms to stay on. Ending a bout early beats grinding it out.
After a 4×4, one bout feeling like real work is your answer — do that one bout and go home.

evidence.transfer: ASSUMED, and claimed more widely than it has ever been tested. Nobody has run a trial where climbers added easy continuous traversing and anything was measured against a control. The honest case for this session is modest and does not need the folklore: it is cheap time on the wall at an intensity that spends nothing — no hard finger exposure, little skin, recoverable the next day — plus deliberate practice at the two habits every endurance session in this menu is trying to buy, moving economically and shaking out before the pump forces it. After a 4×4 it extends the session's time under light load at close to zero marginal cost. Treat any claim bigger than that as unsupported.
evidence.summary: This is the classic 'ARC'-style traverse — continuous low-intensity climbing, prescribed by Hörst and by the Andersons at 10–30 minutes of easy movement. It is expert consensus with no trial behind it, and its usual selling point is one this plan has already graded REFUTED (see the Why tab): no study has shown easy continuous climbing causes capillarisation, and the largest meta-analysis found low-intensity work produced the smallest capillary gains and none in trained subjects. What is left once the folklore is subtracted is still real: movement volume at genuinely low tissue cost, and practice at pacing, economy and shaking out while mildly pumped. Note the intensity here sits BELOW the 60%-of-max band where Devise 2022 measured endurance actually improving — that band belongs to crimp crawls, which is why the crawls carry that citation and this card does not. This is the easiest climbing session in the menu, graded as time on the wall rather than as a stimulus. The dial is hold size and which sections you climb; the dose is barely pumped, never fighting.

Thompson et al. 2015, Eur J Sport Sci (capillary adaptation exists in climbers; no causal training trial)
Devise et al. 2022, Front Sports Act Living 4:862782 (the 60%-of-max band this session deliberately sits below)

dailyMenu.name: ARC laps
dailyMenu.dose: Easy routes on the autobelay, lap after lap, moving the whole time. Two bouts of 20 minutes, 10 minutes sitting between. Three or four number grades below your limit — 5.8s and 5.9s — because the grade is genuinely irrelevant here and the pace is the whole session: a light pump that arrives early and then never changes, no hands-free rests, straight back on after every lower. Count the laps.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Its own session, on any gym visit where you want mileage rather than a stimulus — a low day when the fingers will not take anything hard, a Saturday visit, or the tail of a night that is already spent. Nothing in the prescription depends on what else you did that day: if you are already warm, skip the warm-up and start bout 1, and if the first bout turns into a fight because you have already climbed hard, do that one bout and go home. It is NOT a rest day — 40 minutes of continuous climbing is 40 minutes of work — and it is not a substitute for the hard sessions or for the crawls. Read the evidence block before you spend a whole evening on it: what this buys is cheap time on the wall and pacing practice, and the endurance adaptation it is famous for is one this plan grades REFUTED.

protocol.duration: 50–60 min including warm-up, any gym visit
setup: The autobelay lanes. Better than a rope for this even if you have a partner: no belayer means no waiting, and waiting is the one thing a continuous session cannot afford. The lanes are all vertical, which is fine — vertical is where this belongs.
Two or three routes you can climb without reading them, three to four number grades under your limit. For you that is 5.8–5.9. Pick easy and pick known: thinking about moves is not what you came for.
A clock. The bout is 20 minutes whether or not it feels like 20 minutes, and workout mode runs it and beeps at the end.
Something to count laps with, or just remember the number and put it in the log. The lap count is this session's only hard number.
Chalk sparingly. Forty minutes of hold contact is the most skin this session can cost you and dry skin lasts longer than chalked skin.
warmup: Two laps on the easiest thing on the wall, deliberately slow, a couple of minutes apart.
Two minutes sitting, then start bout 1.
Already warm from something else? Go straight in — this session needs no separate warm-up when the shoulders and fingers are already moving.

blocks.name: A · The bouts — 20 minutes of moving, twice
steps: 1. Climb your route at an even, unhurried pace. Ride the belay down, step straight back on, go again. The ground is a transition of a few seconds, not a rest.
2. Keep that going for the full 20 minutes. Any route, any colour, switch lanes whenever you like — the only rule is that you are moving.

3. INTENSITY, which IS the session: a light pump that arrives in the first five minutes and then sits exactly where it is. Building towards a fight means climb slower, take the bigger holds, or drop a grade mid-bout. Feeling nothing at all after ten minutes means take the worse holds or skip the best ones — not climb faster.

4. No hands-free rests, no parking on a jug to let the pump drain. Continuous light load is the whole prescription, and three 30-second rests turn a 20-minute bout into 18 minutes of climbing and a different session.

5. DOWN-CLIMBING is the cheapest way to make a bout harder without making it harder: instead of riding the belay down, reverse the route. Twice the time on the wall per lap, no increase in peak force, and it is the single best drill for the footwork you cannot see. Mark those laps as up + down in the log — they count as two lengths.
5. Count the laps and write the number down. Same routes, same 20 minutes, more laps in a month is the only progression this session has that is not a feeling.
6. 10 minutes sitting down between bouts, then bout 2. Two bouts is today's dose.
7. WHERE IT GOES when 2×20 stops being work: 2×25, then 3×20, then 3×25, then 3×30 — and stop there. 3×30 is the Andersons' own ceiling and there is nothing behind going past it.

blocks.name: B · Two honest departures from the textbook
steps: THE REST. The Rock Climber's Training Manual rests as long as it works — 20 to 30 minutes between bouts, which makes 2×20 a two-hour evening. Yours is 10 minutes, because at this intensity the rest is not the stimulus and a session you will not finish is worth nothing. If you ever do have a spare evening and want the book's version, take the longer rest; nothing about the bouts changes.

THE GRADE. Hörst says three or four number grades below limit and 30–60 minutes continuous; the Andersons say a moderate but sustainable pump for upwards of 30 minutes on vertical to slightly overhanging terrain, and tell you to avoid hands-free rests. Those two agree on everything that matters here and neither has a trial behind it. Where they disagree with your own experience, believe your forearms: the pump holding steady for the whole bout is the target, and the grade is only the dial you turn to get there.

cues: Even pace beats fast laps. You are buying minutes of light load, not distance up the wall.
Straight back on. The seconds after the lower are where this session quietly leaks.
A steady pump, never a fight. This is the one climbing session in the menu that is supposed to stay a long way from failure — the crawls are where you go near it.
Feet first, silent, long arms. Forty minutes of continuous easy climbing is forty minutes of technique practice whether you intended it or not.
If you are watching the minutes instead of counting the laps, the grade is too hard.
stopIf: Any finger pain. On holds this size a finger complaint means you arrived already damaged — stop the session, do not finish the bout.
A bout turns into something you are surviving rather than sustaining. End the session on the bout you are on; an ARC bout you had to battle was not an ARC bout.
Skin reading 4/5 before you start, or going thin mid-session. Forty minutes of laps is a lot of hold contact and this is the least valuable session in the menu to spend skin on.
Elbow or shoulder ache building lap on lap. High-volume easy pulling is exactly how those two arrive, and they arrive slowly enough that you have to stop on the ache rather than on the pain.
log: Laps per bout — the app adds them up for the chart, so log them where you climbed them
Minutes per bout (workout mode records them)

OPTIONAL: 'log each lap' records the route's grade, whether you fell, and whether you DOWN-CLIMBED it — a lap you climbed and reversed is two lengths of the wall and the chart counts it as two. Nobody expects the detail on a 20-minute bout of 5.8s; it is there for the laps worth remembering.

how.gist: Easy laps on the autobelay, back to back, for twenty minutes.
steps: Pick a route three or four grades under your limit. 5.8–5.9.
Climb it at an even pace, ride the belay down, step straight back on.
Keep moving for the full 20 minutes — any route, any lane, no hands-free rests.
Light pump that never changes. Too much: slower, bigger holds. Too little: worse holds.
Count your laps. Then sit down for 10 minutes and do it again.
how.watch: A jug rest to let the pump drain turns the bout into laps with breaks — the point is that it never stops.
how.easier: Drop a grade, climb slower, or cut the bout to 15 minutes. A shorter bout you climbed continuously beats a long one with rests in it.

evidence.transfer: ASSUMED, and the assumption is one this plan grades REFUTED in the Why tab — read that entry before you build a block around this session. The famous mechanism, that easy continuous climbing grows forearm capillaries, has never been tested: climbers do show real microvascular adaptation (Thompson 2015 measured capillary filtration capacity, an in-vivo index of perfused capillary surface area, higher in climbers than controls), but no trial has ever shown ARC CAUSES it, and the largest meta-analysis on capillary growth found low-intensity work produced the smallest gains and none at all in already-trained subjects. What is left is worth having and is smaller than the folklore: 40 minutes of climbing at a tissue cost near zero, deliberate practice at pacing and economy for longer than any other session in the menu gives you, and — because it is on ropes at 45 ft — practice at the thing the trip actually asks for, which is climbing continuously at an easy grade without bleeding grip. Judge it as mileage, not as a stimulus. The endurance adaptation with a controlled trial behind it lives in the 60%-of-max intermittent band (Devise 2022), which is the crimp crawls, not this.
evidence.summary: The protocol here is the standard one, from two sources that agree and neither of which has run a trial. Anderson & Anderson (The Rock Climber's Training Manual) prescribe base-fitness climbing at a moderate but sustainable pump for upwards of 30 minutes on vertical to slightly overhanging terrain, no hands-free rests, and Uphill Athlete's write-up of the same method gives the numbers this card is built on: 2×30 min with equal rest progressing to 3×25 and then 3×30, twice a week. Hörst (Training for Climbing) prescribes the same thing as 30–60 minutes continuous, three to four number grades below limit, deliberately short of a real pump. Both are expert consensus with no controlled evidence. THE ONE TRIAL that has actually dosed low-intensity climbing did it at 2×10 min, 3×/week for 5 weeks: Held et al. 2023 (Eur J Sport Sci, n=15 trained climbers) used exactly that as the CONTROL arm against the same climbing with blood-flow restriction, and the restricted group came out ahead on grip endurance (+21 s, 95% CrI −2 to 43) and elbow-flexor endurance (+11 s, −5 to 27) with strength changes indistinguishable between arms. Note the credible intervals cross zero — that is a small study — but the direction is worth knowing: when someone did put easy climbing in a trial, plain easy climbing was the comparison that lost. So the honest reading is that the volume in this card (2×20 building to 3×30) is four to nine times the only dose anyone has tested, on the authority of two books rather than a result.
sources: Anderson & Anderson, The Rock Climber's Training Manual (ARC / base fitness — expert consensus, no trial)
Hörst, Training for Climbing (30–60 min continuous, 3–4 grades below limit — expert consensus, no trial)
Devise et al. 2022, Front Sports Act Living 4:862782 (the 60%-of-max band that DOES have a trial)
Thompson et al. 2015, Eur J Sport Sci (microvascular adaptation exists in climbers; no causal training trial)
Liu/Hellsten/Gliemann 2022, Med Sci Sports Exerc (capillary growth meta-analysis: least from low intensity)

dailyMenu.name: Abrahangs — low-intensity no-hangs
dailyMenu.dose: 20mm edge on the Port-A-Board at roughly 40% of max: 10 s on, 20 s off, twenty pulls rotating through six grip positions, once a day. Read the evidence note before you pick this — it is largely the same stimulus as the sub-threshold hang under a more famous name, and the one thing that genuinely distinguishes it is the twice-daily dosing you must not use.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Use this INSTEAD OF — never in addition to — the sub-threshold hang or the unilateral block set, on a Tuesday, Friday or Sunday. Those three sessions are a mutually exclusive set; picking two of them in a day is how a rest week becomes a load week without any session ever feeling hard. Choose the Abrahang specifically when you want the GRIP-POSITION ROTATION — four-finger, front three, front two, middle two — for skin variety and hold-reading, which neither of the other two gives you. Choose the sub-threshold hang instead when you want more time under tension, and the unilateral block set when you want a force target you can actually see on the gauge rather than a load you are guessing by how much weight your feet are taking. Do NOT run it twice a day: that is the actual Abrahamsson protocol and the actual mechanism, and it is also fourteen finger exposures a week in exactly the subgroup where fingerboarding was associated with finger pain. Do NOT run it on a rest day — the rest day card already says not to 'just do a few easy hangs,' and it is right. Do NOT use the 12/10/8mm edges for it. And skip it entirely inside 24 hours of Monday or Thursday, or on any day the fingers feel stiff.

evidence.transfer: Transfer to CLIMBING is not demonstrated, and transfer to TENDON is not even measured. The only outcome study reports a strength-to-weight change; it contains no ultrasound, no biopsy, no stiffness measurement, and no injury data — the authors list all of those as future work. The connective-tissue rationale is entirely extrapolated from Paxton et al. (2012), which measured ERK1/2 phosphorylation and collagen content in an engineered ligament made of human ACL fibroblasts in a fibrin gel: signal peaked at 10 minutes, returned toward baseline by 60, and was refractory for about 6 hours; 10 min of stretch every 6 h for 7 days gave 5.9% collagen vs 4.8% for continuous and 3.1% for control. Baar themselves describes that construct as developmentally immature, more cellular, less matrix-rich and far weaker than adult tissue. Every step from there to your A2 pulley is assumed: that the 6-hour window exists in vivo, that it exists in a finger, that it exists in an adult, and that dish-collagen percentage means tendon stiffness or force-transfer capacity. Be equally honest about the strength claim: the effect was +2.5% strength-to-weight, about +1.8 kg of added load, and it did not reach significance. What this session is actually FOR is grip-position rotation, warm-up quality and near-zero recovery cost. If it does nothing, no existing evidence would have predicted otherwise.
evidence.summary: One study: Gilmore, Klimek, Abrahamsson & Baar (2024, Sports Medicine – Open 10:125). Retrospective mining of Crimpd app logs, n=526 enrolled and 516 analysed after outlier removal, split into climbing-only, Abrahangs-only, max-hangs-only and both. Abrahangs-only changed strength-to-weight by +2.5% (median 3.1%), which did NOT reach significance against climbing alone (p=0.1216, Cohen's d 0.29). Max hangs alone gave +3.2% (p=0.0005, d=0.45) and doing both gave +5.8% (d=0.79, p=0.0081 vs Abrahangs, p=0.0065 vs max hangs). So the widely repeated 'Abrahangs are as effective as max hangs' is a failure to reject the null between two groups, one of them the smallest arm in the study — no equivalence test was run — and the arm in question could not even beat climbing-only. It is also retrospective, self-reported, unrandomised, has no injury outcomes, and states outright that 'we do not know the load used by those in the Abrahangs group' because the weight taken off the feet was self-regulated and unmeasured. The protocol's inventor and the app's designer are both co-authors. Note also that the version with data behind it is 18–22mm at ~40%, not the 14mm at 70–80% of the original videos.

setup: 20mm edge on the Port-A-Board, either hung and standing with feet on the ground, or clipped inline with the Tindeq and pulled against a floor anchor. NOT the 12/10/8mm edges — small edges raise pulley stress per unit of force, which is the exact opposite of the point.

Set the load three ways and take the LOWEST: (a) half your best max-hang total, times 0.40; (b) whatever force you could hold for about 60 seconds with only mild sensation; (c) 40–60% of bodyweight as a total, halved per hand.
Calibrate once on the Tindeq so you know what the number feels like, then reproduce it by feel. Re-measure every 2–3 weeks to confirm you are still at ~40% and not at 60%.
Write the two-finger load down separately. It is roughly half the four-finger load, and it is not optional — 40% of your four-finger max is nowhere near 40% of your two-finger max.
warmup: 1 min: shake the hands out, 10 wrist circles each way, 20 band flexion-extension reps.
Two easy 5-second pulls at about half the target. If the target feels heavy on the second one, your fingers are not recovered — do not train today.

blocks.name: The twenty pulls
steps: Every rep is 10 seconds on, 20 seconds off. Twenty reps total, in six blocks:
1. Four-finger half crimp — 6 reps at the target load.
2. Front three (index, middle, ring), open or drag — 6 reps, same load.
3. Front two, open — 2 reps at HALF the load.
4. Middle two, open — 2 reps at half.
5. Front two, half crimp — 2 reps at half.
6. Middle two, half crimp — 2 reps at half.
7. The standard for the whole session is 'light strain, no pump, could have held it three times as long.' If you are thinking about whether it is too heavy, it is too heavy.

8. HOW TO KNOW IT IS WORKING: honestly, you cannot. The published effect was +2.5% with a between-subject spread of ±7.9% — the noise is three times the signal, so a single person retesting has no ability to attribute anything to this. Track soft signals only: less morning finger stiffness, a shorter warm-up to feeling ready, and no accumulating tweakiness across the block. Anyone who says they felt it working is reporting their expectations.
9. FREQUENCY: once a day, three to five days a week, at least 6 hours clear of any other finger loading, and never within 24 hours of Monday or Thursday.

cues: 'Light strain, no pump.' A pump means the load is too high, full stop.
'Half the load for two fingers.' The most likely way to turn this into an injury is applying the four-finger number to a two-finger grip.

'Once, not twice.' The twice-daily version is the one with the mechanism and the one your exposure budget forbids. You are running the safe half of the protocol and getting the smaller half of the benefit — that is the deal.
'If it costs you anything, it is not worth it.' The whole case for this session is that it is free. The moment it shows up in Monday's numbers, it has stopped being free.
stopIf: You get a forearm pump — the load is too high. Drop 3 kg next session.
Any finger feels tender, hot or tweaky during or after.
Any soreness along the base of a finger.
Your Monday max hang or Thursday board performance drops. This session's only justification is zero interference; if it interferes, it has no reason to exist.
It is within 24 hours of Monday or Thursday, or it is a rest day.
You are tempted to do it a second time today.

RPE — should be 2 or 3; anything above 4 means the dose is wrong

dailyMenu.name: Bouldering with friends
dailyMenu.dose: Climbing for the reason you started. No prescription, no targets — go, jump around on things, try what looks good. Log it honestly afterwards and put the one slider where the night actually landed, because a social evening and an accidental limit session are the same card and very different weeks.
dailyMenu.whenInstead: Pick this whenever it is what you actually want to do — it is the single most likely session in this menu to keep you climbing in five years, and nothing in this plan outranks that. Add it as an EXTRA alongside your main session when you are climbing socially after your real work, and swap it in as your MAIN when the session is the whole evening. The only thing that matters here is honest logging: if you spent the night on a project and pulled hard, move the intensity slider to 4 and the app will count it as a hard finger day, because it was one. That is the trap this card exists to catch — 'just bouldering with friends' is how a two-hard-day week quietly becomes a four-hard-day week, and every finger injury in climbing is preceded by a session nobody counted. Skip it, or keep it at intensity 1–2, within 24 hours either side of Monday and Thursday.

evidence.transfer: Nothing about this session needs justifying on physiological grounds, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. There is no trial showing that social bouldering improves redpoint grade, and there does not need to be — climbing volume is how movement skill is acquired, and movement skill is the largest uncontrolled variable in every training study in this plan. What IS worth stating precisely is the risk side: the injury literature is consistent that overuse accounts for 39–68% of climbing injuries, and unstructured sessions are the ones that go uncounted. The whole design of this card — a required intensity slider that rewrites the day's load level — exists because the accounting matters more than the programming here.
evidence.summary: This is the session with the least evidence behind it and the strongest reason to keep it. Adherence is the only training variable with a guaranteed effect size: a plan you abandon in week 4 has an effect of zero, and the plan's own menu note already names that failure mode. The relevant literature is not performance research but injury epidemiology: Zieliński et al. (2025, systematic review, 7 studies, >4000 climbers) put climbing injury incidence at 2.7–4.44 per 1000 hours with overuse making up 39–68% of injuries, and risk rising in dose-dependent fashion with grade and with years climbing. Sjöman et al. (2023) found finger pain positively associated with fingerboarding specifically in the subgroup you sit in — male, fewer than six years climbing, performing around 7a+. Neither of those is an argument against climbing for fun. Both are arguments for counting it.

setup: None. That is the point.
One thing only: decide before you walk in whether this is your main session or an extra on top of one. That decision is the difference between a good week and a third hard finger day.
warmup: Warm up anyway. The injury risk in a social session is not the climbing, it is pulling hard on a cold finger twenty minutes in because someone showed you a good problem.
10 minutes of easy movement before you try anything that feels hard.

blocks.name: Climb
steps: Go climbing. There is no protocol here and adding one would ruin it.
Afterwards, do the only part that matters: put the slider where the night actually landed. It used to be two sliders asking the same question in two scales — it is one now, 1 to 10.
1–3 — social. You mostly talked. Barely climbed.
4–5 — easy volume. Lots of moving, nothing near your limit.
6–7 — you worked some things. Real load, some hard attempts, not a limit session.
8+ — you tried hard. Projecting, repeated max attempts, pumped and fully committed. This counts as a hard finger day and the app will treat it as one.
Be honest at 7 versus 8. That boundary is the whole value of this card, and it is the line the app actually reads.

cues: 'Log what happened, not what you planned.' The slider is the entire job.
'If you are projecting, it is an 8.' Not a 7 because it was social.

protocol.duration: 35–40 min including warm-up. This is your one long day.
setup: Basement board. 20mm rung for the work, 25/30mm for warm-up.

Have your MVC-7 number written down. Every load below is a percentage of it.

Now that you have the Tindeq you can anchor this properly: measure a 6-second max pull PER HAND on the Port-A-Board, sum both hands, and work at 80% of that summed figure with the live force readout, ending each set when you can no longer produce 70%. warmup: 2 min: shake the arms out, wrist circles both directions, open and close the fists 20×.

3 × 10s on the 25mm at roughly half your max, 60s rest between. Feet lightly assisting is fine.
1 × 7s on the 20mm at about 70%. Then rest 3 FULL minutes, sitting down.
Do not skip the 3 minutes. Skipping it turns your max test into an endurance test.

blocks.name: A · Max hangs — protect the engine
steps: 3 sets × 7 seconds on the 20mm, two hands, half crimp. (Reduced from 4 — you need something left for block B.)

Half crimp means fingers bent to roughly 90° at the middle knuckle, thumb off the board.
Arms slightly bent, shoulders pulled DOWN and back. Never hang dead off the joints.
If you cannot hold a clean 7 seconds on set 2, stop the whole session here. That still counts.

blocks.name: B · Repeaters — set the load by completion, not by percentage
steps: REST 8 FULL MINUTES after the last max hang. Not 3. The source protocol used 8 minutes between sets and it matters.

Set the load so you can complete 8–12 reps with the last one clean. On 20mm that will almost certainly mean COUNTERWEIGHT — taking weight off with the pulley, not adding it. That is correct and expected, not a sign you are weak.
10 seconds on, 6 seconds off. Hands OFF the board between reps, arms by your sides.
END THE SET when your force visibly drops or your fingers roll open from half crimp — not at a rep count.
2 sets, 8 minutes between them.
Write down the load you actually used. That number, not a percentage, is what you progress week to week — add a little only when you can finish both sets cleanly at 12 reps.

Weight into the fingers, not the arms — you are not doing a pull-up.

reframe.title: What you are actually training for
reframe.body: You are not training to climb 5.12a for 80 feet. Read the route descriptions: on a typical sport 5.12a the hard climbing is one short crux, and most of the route is 5.10 or 5.10+ with a rest or two. You are training to climb 5.10+/5.11- efficiently for about 50 feet without bleeding 20% of your grip, arrive at one named rest, actually recover there, and then execute a 3–6 move boulder problem around V3–V4. The trainable gap is not overgripping the filler, and recovering enough at one rest to reset.

Skip the next HARD exposure, not the daily habit. Drop to sub-threshold. Still there after 48h? Three days off finger loading entirely.
